pool.titulo: The GTAs that are still worth playing while you wait for GTA 6 on PC
pool.resumen: I bet GTA 6 doesn't even have a jetpack.
pool.contenido:
Play This Right Now Welcome to Play This Right Now, the site version of our weekly newsletter in which we celebrate a new game, update, or DLC that we think is well worth checking out. You can subscribe to the newsletter at the link if you want to get our thoughts about a new videogame happening direct to your inbox every Thursday.
The big day has been and gone, but you and me? We're locked out in the cold. Grand Theft Auto 6 is enthralling a gazillion console owners across the globe, but those of us loyal to our desktops (or, perhaps, without the means to buy a console to play the thing on) are waiting for its practically certain PC port, may it come sooner rather than later.
But you know what? Who cares! If you want a GTA fix on PC, you've still got plenty of options to choose from. Here are PC Gamer's three biggest criminals to tell you what you should be playing while we wait for Rockstar to get its act together.
Grand Theft Auto 4 Is there any sentence in GTA more iconic than "Cousin, let's go bowling!" Growing up, GTA was a game about rampaging, about stealing tanks, helicopters, and seeing how many cops you could slaughter by holing up in some building site, or making a last stand on the freeway. It was never a game I expected to make me feel something.
But GTA 4 has the best story in the series—a quintessential rags-to-riches narrative that, through Nico's perspective as an immigrant to Liberty City, is the most thorough exploration of the American Dream (arguably, the theme in GTA) that the games have ever managed. It's got that satirical bite, but it's perhaps the first and only time GTA ever properly pulled off those heartbreaking RPG-style choices that genuinely surprise you.
It's a wonderfully paced game which sees Nico ascend the heights of Liberty City's criminal ladder, plus it's got some excellent DLC, which Rockstar used to flesh out other characters in the city. But while its missions still stand up, its silliest moments are often the most memorable, like stumbling out of a bar after getting drunk with your cousin and trying to drive home without killing you both. That, or its wild array of cheats and mods, like the one that makes traffic 9999999% faster .
Grand Theft Auto 5 GTA 5 has had more room to breathe than any other game in the series—13 whole years!—and that sort of overexposure can make it easy to forget just how good this one is.
Intertwining the stories of three protagonists meant there was always a slightly different vibe you could go for—Franklin's fresher, more humble small-time gang origins, Michael's rich suburban life which belies marital issues and a yearning to return to criminal glory, and… well, Trevor. Who you'll dive in to play as, only to discover he's ended up in a dumpster wearing a dress.
Seamlessly switching between each character and feeling like they'd actually continued to live beyond being at the behest of your inputs was rad, especially when it came to the myriad of heists sprinkled across the story that required you to jump between each character and tackle different roles.
While its story isn't the strongest, it more than makes up for that in vibes. Los Santos is a dream to drive through , its radio stations are some of the best the series has seen, and there's always something to stop and do—be it a quick ATM robbery or a chill game of tennis.
Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas We are now in a post-GTA 6 world and yet, somehow, Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas still feels like the most ambitious game Rockstar ever made. It is the culmination of the GTA 3 saga: the summit of a mountain we all started climbing in 2001, when that one guy told us his hands were all messed up so we better drive (brother).
It is Rockstar operating at the full mastery of its engine and its target platform, and as a result it bristles with little touches and systems that were nowhere to be seen in GTA 3 and Vice City. Want to get jacked? Hit the gym. Want to get hefty? Hit the pizza place. Want to have sex? Download a shady-ass mod.
You've got territory control, skill-training, extensive character customisation, a huge and diverse map, Tom Petty on the soundtrack—there is simply a huge amount of game here, and arranged in such a way that I genuinely think Rockstar still hasn't quite pulled off since. No, being able to get slightly paunchy in RDR2 doesn't count; absolute unit or bust.
With the original version of San Andreas (rather slimily) removed from Steam to prod people towards buying the Definitive Edition, your options are either to pick up the latter or buy the OG trilogy on the Rockstar games store . Frankly, I'd recommend the Definitive Edition. San Andreas is excellent enough to outshine its remaster's deficiencies, and the modernised controls are pretty handy. And hey, we're on PC—there are ways and means to restore what's missing .

pool.titulo: Grand Theft Auto 6 has a 'complex drug network' that tracks everything from where drugs come from to 'how they eventually reach the street-level buyer'
pool.resumen: "Having that structure in the background as something we consistently refer to helps everything feel more real."
pool.contenido:
I've only dipped my toe into Grand Theft Auto 6 thus far, but I'm already impressed by the detail Rockstar has baked into its world. One thing I'm always curious about with games like this, however, is how much of that detail is on the surface versus what's actually happening under the hood.
I'm still too early in the game to judge this for myself, but according to Rockstar, there is way more going on in terms of how NPCs behave than players will ever likely see. One striking example of this is how GTA 6's gang compounds conduct their drug operations. In an interview with IGN , Rockstar's senior design director for its open world Steven Messinger explained that GTA 6 fully simulates drug distribution from top to bottom.
"A big part of [the open world's design] was establishing deep backstories for almost everything, even if they were never meant to be fully explained to the player, and then really sticking to those backstories," Messinger pointed out. "For example, our gang compounds have a complex drug network we've fully mapped out: where the drugs come from, who brings them in and how, how they're distributed to each compound, what happens at each stop, and how they eventually reach the street-level buyer."
Messinger notes that "players will only pick up bits and pieces of this". But representing this process wholesale means that, when players do notice it, it always feels authentic and believable. "Having that structure in the background as something we consistently refer to helps everything feel more real, like this big machine is always running even when players aren't there."
While this may only be designed for players to notice passively, I'm now keen to follow this system and see just how consistently it holds up. But it's such commitment to representing its world that has led GTA 6 to receive near-universal praise from critics, and it probably didn't hurt when it earned $3.79 billion on launch day , either.

pool.titulo: The designer of Atari's notorious E.T. likens the deluge of AI games to events that preceded the '80s industry crash: 'There was a glut of crap on the market'
pool.resumen: Despite this, Howard Scott Warshaw thinks AI will be a "super positive thing" for the industry.
pool.contenido:
The emergence of generative AI coding tools has numerous effects on the games industry this year, but the prominent of these is that it's made Steam an absolute nightmare to navigate . Since the summer, Steam (and other storefronts like itch.io) have been inundated with clones and AI slop games , as AI users turn to tools like Claude to output thousands of low-quality titles.
For many of us, this seems like a new problem. But for one veteran game developer, the scenario is all too familiar. Howard Scott Warshaw is the developer of numerous Atari 2600 games including Yars' Revenge and Raiders of the Lost Ark. But perhaps his most famous (or infamous) game is 1982's E.T. the Extra Terrestrial, the notorious tie-in game that was so terrible Atari buried unsold copies of it in the desert .
E.T. has been cited as a contributing factor in the US video game industry crash of 1983—one of many poor-quality 8-bit titles that hollowed out the gaming market in the States. It's here where Warshaw sees a parallel to today's emerging scenario, though he doesn't necessarily believe it will end in the same way.
In a talk he gave at the DevGAMM Lisbon conference last week (via GamesIndustry.biz ) Warshaw remarked upon how AI coding tools have seemed to rapidly sped up iteration times on game development. "People who used to spend weeks, months or years programming something can now do it in days with AI support," he explained.
"So what does this mean in game development? What it means is we're going to see a lot more games produced. You ever hear of the crash of '83 or '84, the big video game crash? They said the problem that happened in the crash, and I think that was true, was there was a glut of crap on the market, because the machine opened up and anybody could just pop a game out, and they did."
Warshaw pointed out that, at the time "good games were still being made" but these games were "way overshadowed by the crap: and that created a real problem in the game industry." He sees a similar situation emerging now thanks to generative AI tools. "AI is going to have the same impact on a larger scale, because on one level, so many more people can now realise and create a video game than ever could before just using AI. And that's okay, but there's going to be a lot of crap, because most games suck. That's just the way it is."
The reason for this, Warshaw says, is that, like all artistic endeavours "there's some things in life that everybody can see themselves doing, and the truth is most people who do it can't do it very well. And what AI is going to do is make that more possible for people who can't do it to do it." Yet while he thinks that most of the games that result from these ideas "aren't going to be very interesting" he also believes that "it's also going to enable the people who really do have some innovative, interesting and solid ideas to realise those, too."
In short, Warshaw believes that AI will provoke a shift away from technology development to a greater focus on game design, which he ultimately believes is "actually going to be a super positive thing for the video game industry." He also said that, despite observing similar warning signs as in 1983, he doesn't "see the prospect of a crash in the video game industry" and instead expects to see a "reorganisation, where we need better filters to figure out a way to get rid of the garbage games".
Warshaw is certainly correct about AI tools resulting in a flood of crap, but I also think he himself overvalues the inherent worth of ideas in terms of what makes a great game. While ideas themselves can be inherently good or bad, no idea emerges from the creative process unscathed. Indeed, a major factor in creating art of any kind is engaging and grappling with that process, learning how to deal with the friction between the image in your head and what ends up on the page, or the canvas, or your scripting program. That mastery only comes through practice and experience. It cannot be outsourced or circumvented.
But that doesn't change the fact that storefronts are currently being overwhelmed with terrible, AI-assisted games, and it's having all manner of knock-on effects. Earlier this month, Valve admitted it is "running behind" on approving Steam games because it has to keep re-reviewing them, and although Valve didn't cite AI as the cause of this, it's an awful coincidence that this has started happening as AI coding tools result in game submissions shooting through the roof.

pool.titulo: Jason's stoic character in Grand Theft Auto 6 was inspired by Steve McQueen and research into Army veterans: 'These guys typically aren't running their mouths'
pool.resumen: Rockstar made a point of creating "authentic characters that didn't stray too far from reality."
pool.contenido:
It's already clear that Grand Theft Auto 6 has a very different timbre than most other GTA games. While criminal hijinks and acerbic satire remain part of the experience, it's also much more interested in portraying characters and relationships in a more convincing, human fashion.
One of the most striking examples of this is its depiction of co-protagonist Jason Duval, who, unlike the vast majority of GTA's main characters, is often notable for what he doesn't say rather than what he does. According to Rockstar's senior vice president of narrative Rupert Humphries, Jason's laconic nature was inspired by a personality type observed in both cinema and real-life.
"When we decided we wanted to tell a story about a couple on the run, we looked at all the similar kinds of movies, and one of the ones that really stood out was [Sam] Peckinpah's The Getaway" Humphries explained in a statement given to Destructoid (via GamesRadar ). Steve McQueen was famous for pulling lines out of scripts and saying things with his presence alone. We wanted to see how close we could get to that with a game character, where so many of our protagonists have been the opposite."
Humphries says this also "resonated" with research the studio was doing around Army veterans, particularly Army Rangers. In Grand Theft Auto 6, Duval is a veteran of the game's equivalent military organisation called the Marauders. "These guys typically aren't running their mouths or reacting to something unless it's strictly necessary, while still being strong and still asserting themselves," Humphries explained.
Establishing a more grounded character was not solely a directive for Jason. It was a goal of the writing more broadly. This is interesting considering Florida was picked as the setting for GTA 6 in-part due to the wild 'Florida Man' stories that circulate on the Internet from the state. "Researching the prolific and headline-grabbing criminal activity that had been taking place over decades in Florida was an obvious starting point," game writer Michael Wiafe pointed out.
"From then on, it was about coming up with authentic characters that didn't stray too far from reality but also were not totally bound by it either," Wiafe continues. "The majority of our main characters are undeniably reprehensible on paper, full-blown criminals, but also decent human beings. Their moral makeup isn’t necessarily cut-and-dry, and we don’t attempt to make excuses for them. What's important is how they resonate, no matter where you're experiencing the game in the world."
This is just one of the things that makes Rockstar's latest crime sim a marvel on pretty much all fronts . And while us PC gamers will have to wait an unspecified amount of time before it arrives on the platform, you can bet it going to be quite the experience when it does.

pool.titulo: Astarion's Baldur's Gate 3 prequel novel infuriated fans, now it's Shadowheart's turn
pool.resumen: Her book's being written by award-winning author Tasha Suri.
pool.contenido:
Tasha Suri, author of the Burning Kingdoms trilogy and several other books, will be writing Baldur's Gate 3: Shadowheart, the official BG3books website has announced. Another prequel to Larian's videogame, this one focuses on Shadowheart's time as a priestess in the Church of Shar, and is about a murder mystery.
"When a member of their order is killed in the Upper City," the blurb goes, "Shadowheart and her so-called allies are called to investigate. She trusts none of them: not Mirie, the ambitious Griefguard; not Caldan, the cynical propagandist; and certainly not Nocturne, the charming quartermistress, who claims to have only Shadowheart’s best interests in mind."
Mirie and Nocturne are both characters you can meet in Baldur's Gate 3, while Caldan Darkwood is mentioned in a note you can find . Nocturne in particular has a close relationship with Shadowheart, which could be interesting to see developed. "Torn between the familiar comforts of the dark and the thrill of new desire," the blurb continues, "she must solve the mystery to prove her devotion… or be cast into the light."
Which sounds fine and dandy, but it'll have an uphill battle with the Baldur's Gate 3 fandom, who've been vocally critical of the Astarion novel for its lightness of tone—especially given his traumatic backstory—and apparently mischaracterizing Astarion and his sire, Cazador, as well as being inaccurate to the lore.
I haven't read the Astarion book, but I did read the original Baldur's Gate novels, which were terrible. So were almost all the D&D books I read in a youthful post-Tolkien haze where I'd put up with anything that had wizards in it. My expectations are pretty low, but I do like to slip a trashy fantasy novel between heavier reads as a palate-cleanser so maybe I'll try this one some day.
Baldur's Gate 3: Shadowheart will be out in a 304-page hardcover edition and in ebook form on June 8, as well as a 10-hour audiobook. The Astarion audiobook was read by Astarion performer Neil Newbon, we'll have to wait and see if Jennifer English reads the Shadowheart book.
If the series continues I could see a Wyll prequel being interesting, since he gets a bit short-changed in the videogame, though I wouldn't expect it to sell as well as novels about the more popular companions.

pool.titulo: Comcast: 'At peak, GTA 6 accounted for nearly a quarter of all internet traffic'
pool.resumen: November 19 marked the highest-traffic day in the ISP's history.
pool.contenido:
In a post to X, "The Everything App," US entertainment and communications conglomerate Comcast revealed that Grand Theft Auto 6's historic launch drove record-breaking internet traffic. According to Comcast, only a quarter of "the entire internet" was downloading Rockstar's latest cozy game phenomenon .
"GTA 6 didn't just break records in gaming," Comcast wrote. "Its launch drove the biggest internet traffic day in our network history, with traffic climbing 31% above an average day. At peak, GTA 6 accounted for nearly a quarter of all network traffic."
Comcast shared a video of a line graph showing the massive relative spike in activity on November 19. The chart is unlabeled except for the date, but it presumably corresponds to the volume of data being downloaded across Comcast's entire network.
And that last but does add a caveat to the numbers Comcast cited: Its network and "the entire internet" are two different things, unless I'm missing something here or Comcast's data accounts for other ISPs and other countries, not just its own services.
Regardless, it's still a significant bit of fun with statistics, another example of the totalizing footprint of what may be the largest commercial launch in entertainment history . Imagine how much bigger it would have been launching on PC as well.

pool.titulo: The team behind Ubisoft's 'first playable AI-based R&D project' has been established as its own subsidiary called Motherbrain
pool.resumen: In the name of "more immersive and engaging player experiences," of course.
pool.contenido:
Use of generative AI in game dev remains as contentious as it does ubiquitous— a recent GDC report found that around 40% of devs use AI, but more than half think its influence has been negative. Ubisoft is continuing to double down on the technology , this time with Motherbrain, a new subsidiary fashioned from the team behind its "first playable generative AI experience."
As reported by VGC , Motherbrain's purpose is to develop "AI for gameplay innovation, supporting all game creators in developing groundbreaking experiences … Its current focus is on new player experiences, smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large scale systemic worlds," according to an earnings report which was released Thursday.
The information comes at a turbulent time for the publishing giant, which just laid off 166 employees even after Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced "outperformed expectations." A sweeping internal overhaul earlier this year saw the company reorganize its workforce into a throng of "creative houses," a decision which led to swathes of layoffs and six project cancellations, including the Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time Remake.
It's not clear what Motherbrain are at work on, in specific terms, right now, but there may be some clues in its past work. That playable AI "experience" I mentioned earlier is none other than Teammates, an R&D project based on a prior experiment with uncanny AI "neo-NPCs."
Teammates aimed to allow players to command NPC squadmates in a rudimentary shooter game with a microphone, and using AI, have those squadmates react believably. It's not far off, at least conceptually, from what we've seen in games like Where Winds Meet and Fortnite , both of which have experimented with AI-powered NPCs.

pool.titulo: GTA 6 Protective Custody: Should you choose proceed or postpone when you go to meet Abe?
pool.resumen: Meet with your lawyer or wait and do it later?
pool.contenido:
Deciding whether to proceed or postpone the Protective Custody story mission is a big choice you'll need to make in GTA 6 . The mission appears on your map as "Meet Abe" in Chapter 5, once you've completed the mission Operation Savage Glory.
Once you get to Abe's office, Jason will warn Lucia that everything will change after this mission. Lucia will hesitate at the door as you make your choice to "Proceed" or "Postpone."
This is a pretty big decision, because Protective Custody kicks off the final mission of the game which takes about an hour to play. And even though it's a binary choice between "Proceed" (which starts the mission) and "Postpone" (which delays the mission)" there's actually a third possible outcome based on when you make the choice.
Proceed or Postpone Proceed : Jason and Lucia will enter Abe's office and the final mission of the game will begin. It's a long mission that will take about an hour to play, so be prepared. You can't save during this mission so make sure you've got the time! Once you've completed the final mission, you can watch the credits and return to the open world so you can continue playing.
Postpone : You delay the final mission. You will go back to the open world to continue playing. The "Meet Abe" icon will remain on your map so you can begin the final mission at any point from then on.
The third option:
Proceed with $2 million in your Buck Me savings account There are multiple endings to GTA 6, and I won't spoil them here. But one of the endings is only possible if you postpone the Protective Custody mission until you've deposited $2 million into your Buck Me savings account . That's why when you choose to proceed with the final mission makes a difference.
It's also worth noting (again, without spoilers) that just because you do have $2 million in your Buck Me savings account does not guarantee you will see this particular ending. There are still choices you'll need to make in the final mission that determine which ending you see.

pool.titulo: Skyrim lead chats about the Fallout diehards who hated that Bethesda got the series: 'We had to prove them wrong, and fortunately we did'
pool.resumen: "You can't help but take it a little bit personally".
pool.contenido:
When Bethesda got its hands on the Fallout licence way back in 2004, the naysayers were many and vocal. In fairness, the naysayers are still many and vocal, but they were back then too, and it turns out Bethesda saw at least a few of their posts. In a chat with The Examined Game , Skyrim lead Bruce Nesmith reflected on the reaction some Fallout old-heads had to Bethesda's acquisition of the series.
"There was huge pushback when Bethesda got the Fallout licence to do Fallout 3. There was a lot of people who were Obsidian fans, who were like 'Bethesda's gonna screw it up, they're just gonna make it Skyrim, we want Fallout the way we remember Fallout', and there was a strong, vocal community that just hated that we were gonna make that game".
For clarity's sake, the angry fans at the time were likely Black Isle and Interplay fans rather than Obsidian fans—the latter studio hadn't ever made a Fallout game in 2004 (though it had Fallout alumni on staff), and they were prophesying (after 2006) that Bethesda's take on Fallout would be like Oblivion, not Skyrim, since the latter released in 2011. I suspect Nesmith is muddling the initial negative reaction with, well, the more modern one, which is shaped in large part by Obsidian's excellent Fallout: New Vegas from 2010.
"We had to prove them wrong", recalls Nesmith, "and fortunately we did, because Fallout 3 was embraced even by a lot of our sceptics". It's true: people bloody loved Fallout 3 and still do, though there are of course still series fans who reject the game. "There's always going to be some diehard people that say 'Fallout 2 was the greatest Fallout game ever', but we tried our best to just not engage… because you're not going to win that argument.
"All you can do is make the best game you can and let that be your statement. And that's what Bethesda did".
Does the vitriol ever get to Bethesda and its devs? Unsurprisingly, yeah, a little. "Any time somebody says that the thing you're doing is, you know, fill in your blank for all the cuss words and the bad things… you feel like it's a statement about yourself. You have to divorce yourself from that [but] you can't help but take it a little bit personally. But it does make you want to prove them wrong. It does make you want to say 'I'm going to show you that this will work, that we can respect the franchise and make it better and make it our way, rather than the old way".

pool.titulo: Fake figures seized from dishonest dealer in Shanghai sting spurred by tacky Tifa tchotchke
pool.resumen: Keeping our streets safe.
pool.contenido:
As reported by The Shanghai Observer and Automaton , authorities in Shanghai have arrested 13 people and seized an untold number of unauthorized model kits and figures based on pop culture properties like Final Fantasy. The cops were reportedly put on the trail by a suspect Tifa Lockheart figurine.
Police in Fengxian, a district of Shanghai, began receiving complaints in June. The Shanghai Observer showed pictures comparing a Play Arts Kai (Square Enix's premium figure line) Tifa with a seemingly less articulated counterpart in the same outfit. Reading through machine translation, it sounds like customers in the area bought these figures online expecting the genuine article.
The leader of the operation reportedly commissioned a Guangzhou factory to produce the false Tifa and her ilk. They even sold some figures at higher prices than the genuine article, offering added accessories or features not available in the official product.
I'm of two minds about this, personally: I'm generally pro-kitbashing, selling custom figures, and using proxies in trading card games. In the face of some seriously inflated pricing from official merch lines, bootlegs can often be more enticing than the real deal, particularly if they offer features you can't get from official products⁠—the added customization options from this arrested vendor actually sound weirdly pro-consumer.
But it certainly appears, at least from The Shanghai Observer's reporting, that these suspect figures were being presented as the genuine article to customers. Paired with the increased price vs. official merch, and I find myself soured on the whole operation. It may seem small and silly, but as we endure the Golden Age of Scams, it's weirdly nice to see scammers face some consequences somewhere .

pool.titulo: World of Warcraft: Forever has turned me into a big, friendly golden retriever that says hello to everybody
pool.resumen: I'd almost forgotten what it was like.
pool.contenido:
Terminally Online This is Terminally Online : PC Gamer's very own MMO column. Every other week, I'll be sharing my thoughts on the genre, interviewing fellow MMO-heads like me, taking a deep-dive into mechanics we've all taken for granted, and, occasionally, bringing in guest writers to talk about their MMO of choice.
World of Warcraft: Foreve r's done a lot of things for me over the past couple of weeks—it's given me a deeper appreciation for oldschool MMO quest design, it's wowed me with some genuinely impressive new lighting technology, and it's… ugh, it's made me so friendly.
Mind, I wouldn't say I'm unkind when I play MMOs, but I am a solo player by habit. I'll have a guild, friends I roleplay with, sure. But I'm very rarely striking up conversations with people in-game—all of that typically happens in Discord. And yet, here I am in WoW forever, trying to emphatically start conversations with goddamn everyone I meet.
And it's in part because of how much of a bastard the game is. I don't think Classic is a particularly difficult videogame—I've even gotten my warrior from level 1 to, at the time of writing, 56 as fury, a spec typically considered trash for levelling. And it's been fine, I've just minded my pulls and levelled first aid.
But it is a known fact that vanilla WoW quests are just easier when you group up with people. Part of this is because players are a force multiplier—many classes have group buffs, and not having to worry about health with a healer present means that you can pull swathes of enemies and melt them down easily.
And so I've been doing that. I've been grouping with people, and they've been grouping with me, and… oh, god, we've been talking to each other .
I don't know if I just happen to have a lucky propensity for drawing in nice folks, but my levelling journey has been dappled with some of the chillest people you'll ever meet. People hanging around to help you finish quests they've already completed is so common it's almost standard.
In one instance, a shadow priest carried me through multiple elite quests in Stranglethorn Vale—they needed to do 'em too, sure, but they actively went out of their way to show me where I could get a couple.
There is a real, tangible sense of camaraderie in the game right now, one that's yet to be grinded to the marrow by the efficiency-laden tasks of Mythic+ or a seasonal system. But it's also one borne of how long everything takes. When you've already spent 10 minutes jogging to a quest, what's another five to help a stranger out?
It is, to put it plainly, the opposite of what I'd expected after years of playing far more modern MMOs. I'm even way ahead of the curve of the general population level-wise, and I'm still meeting these relaxed, generous folks. People who'll offer up scraps of a treasure map that's dropping from the pirates we're grinding for free, rather than being a mercenary about it and selling them on the auction house.
Moreover, it is infectious. I've been handing mana potions to people. I've been sticking around to help out with quests—in a recent Zul'farrak run, a dungeon I was only doing twice because I'd missed that it was required for the Sunken Temple questline, our tank had simply atrocious luck collecting troll tempers for a quest (you need 20 of them, and they don't drop often).
Not just myself, but another player in the same situation all stuck around for about 20 minutes just to help them out. When they thanked us, I, saccharine and glowing with the spirit of a reformed Grinch, said: "No worries, bud, if you wanna live in a village you've gotta be a villager sometimes."
Ugh.
In short, Forever's turned me into a big, fluffy, golden-haired dog. The kind you meet in a park that bounds up to you with its stupid tongue wagging out. All that oldschool game design and camaraderie has, as it turns out, been a complete antidote to my hermetic ways. And while my street cred as a tough, solemn badass might never recover, I'm glad to be taking my time.

pool.titulo: The most unforgivable crime in GTA 6 is that TV placement
pool.resumen: Jason and Cal do their best to redecorate the bach' pad but c'mon boys, a TV in front of a giant glass door? We can do better.
pool.contenido:
Grand Theft Auto 6 is a game about criminals doing crimes. Car crimes, gun crimes, drug crimes, and first degree decorating crimes. Early in the game, Jason's buddy Cal convinces him that he's got to turn his r/malelivingspace shack into a place he can bring his girl Lucia without feeling like she's still stuck in a jail cell. Cal is right, but his decorating decisions should be illegal.
This is how Jason's living room looks at the beginning of the game while he's still flying solo. Not great, Jason. If I've learned anything from lurking in interior decorating communities online it's that furniture should never be touching your walls, no matter how small the room is, and that nobody's TV is ever at the right height.
Cal hassles Jason into moving some things around and, while I love his motivation, he makes everything worse. What they wind up with is this: couch blocking prime navigation space and the TV sitting in front of the sliding glass door. Look, I know the point is that Cal is an incompetent dork. He's slugging beers and insisting they make the room feng shui. I can't forgive him for this one though.
Cal does get one thing right here: using the couch and arm chair to create a space that feels like a living room within the open area. Once Lucia moves in she and Jason continue making the waterfront shack more homey. They get a rug in the living room, a classic choice to finish tying that space into a room. Lucia brings home a coffee table to assemble (cute domestic conversation ensues). The dining table gets centered properly in its corner.
But that damn TV stays parked in front of the glass door. It's criminal! There would be so much glare on that screen from the east and west facing windows and light all day long drowning it out from behind that north facing glass door. My sad, myopic eyes are tearing up just thinking about squinting at it.
So I took Jason's conundrum to one of the interior decorating communities on Reddit to ask for some group workshopping. They immediately grasped the unforgivable TV placement and the inherent issue with the number of windows in this place. Almost no wall is safe here.
One suggestion was to keep those window blinds in the living room down and place the TV stand in front of it. Makes sense to me—Jason wouldn't be losing much light with all the other windows in here. Another more minor fix was to just put the TV at a 45 degree angle in its corner so it's less directly in front of the glass door, though I don't think that solves the glare problems.
The more popular suggestion (and my favorite) was to swap the dining and living room. The TV can sit on the rear wall, slightly tucked away with the blinds pulled down, while the dining table gets easier access from the kitchen and doesn't suffer for being lit from all sides.
Alas, I have it on good authority that the TV never manages to move from where Cal stuck it. I can forgive drug smuggling, but I draw the line at suboptimal viewing angles. Ah well, perhaps Jason and Lucia have a better floor plan to work with in the next place they move to as their criminal exploits grow.

pool.titulo: As a kid, I didn't have a monster in my attic, I had a LAN
pool.resumen: I'm not boasting. OK, I am a bit.
pool.contenido:
Weird Weekend Weird Weekend is our regular Saturday column where we celebrate PC gaming oddities: peculiar games, strange bits of trivia, forgotten history. Pop back every weekend to find out what Jeremy, Josh, Rick and Ted have become obsessed with this time, whether it's the canon height of Thief's Garrett or that time someone in the Vatican pirated Football Manager .
Multiplayer gaming on PC these days is so easy you probably barely even think about it. Most games that support multiplayer will work out of the gate, and there's an abundance of ways to connect and chat with your friends across the globe. This is a far cry from the early days of PC multiplayer, when dial-up connections and ad-hoc servers made multiplayer PC gaming expensive and unreliable.
Indeed, the best way to play multiplayer PC games back then was via a LAN. A local network offered the fastest and most stable connections, and didn't cost you anything beyond the hardware required to hook it all together. Unfortunately, it was also the least convenient way of playing PC games with your friends, as it meant one or several of you had to haul your whole-ass PC to an agreed-upon location.
Because of this, LAN gaming was a rare treat for most people in the '90s and early '00s. Unless, that is, you happened to be a disgustingly lucky bastard like myself, and had a LAN in your attic that you could play at any time.
Now, this sounds like the kind of lie a 10-year-old would blurt out in the playground to impress his friends (specifically, an eight-year-old from the mid '90s who had a working knowledge of PC gaming, which, I concede, is a limited demographic) and indeed, the further away I get from that time, the more like a false memory it seems. But it is 100% true, and I have the pictures to prove it.
The LAN (as it was simply and practically known) was in service between 2001 and 2003, and existed because of my family's long-running enthusiasm for PCs and PC gaming. As I've mentioned in other articles, my dad was fascinated by the internet from 1994 onward, both just as a technology and for the business opportunities it offered. Meanwhile, his brother (my uncle) was an IT support expert and a dedicated PC gamer.
Since they were close as siblings and shared this mutual interest (at least on the PC aspect—my dad was never much of a gamer) there was a constant stream of PC hardware flowing through the house, as they tried to keep up with the rapid progress of PCs through the '90s. Eventually, when they'd upgrade a PC, they began taking the old components and building them into a "new" PCs. This is how my brother and I ended with our joint PC in 1997, and how we ended up with individual PCs a few years later.
In 2000 my family (and, separately, my uncle) moved to the Isle of Man, which for non UK audiences is a small island between Britain and Ireland known for two things: tail-less cats and incredibly dangerous motorbike races. The house we rented there had a converted attic—complete with creaky, bare-floorboard stairs—and my dad decided this was the ideal space to set up all three PCs.
Initially the PCs weren't connected. But the layout of the room meant it was only a matter of time before my dad and uncle had that particular brainwave. At some point in 2001, another upgrade happened, and we were left with spare parts for a fourth PC, which could be used as a dedicated server to network the other three PCs together.
The upshot was we had a three-PC LAN on which we could play multiplayer games. I have a distinct memory of them clunking about in the attic while setting this up—likely over a weekend or possibly that year's Easter holiday. I also remember them showing it to us once they were done and explaining how it all worked.
What I don't remember, annoyingly, is what the first game we played on it was. It might have been Doom, though I can't say for certain. I think the reason I don't remember is that once the LAN was set up, my brother and I were largely left to our own devices to get games running on it. Hence, a lot of my memories surrounding the LAN are about that , rather than the games we actually played.
Even with the hard work of setting up the LAN done, getting games to work on it often proved a challenge. Since each PC was the product of multiple rounds of leftovers, they all had different components, so the chance of encountering compatibility issues with a game on at least one of the PCs was not insignificant. The difference between a 1998 PC and a 2001 PC was cavernous, so they might have a processor that was too old, a graphics card that didn't support the latest DirectX, insufficient RAM.
In addition, while we had three PCs, we'd typically only have one copy of any given game, which meant rolling the dice on copy protection with every game we tried (and occasionally searching the murkier corners of the Internet for a crack or a keygen— don't tell the police .) Even if the game installed successfully, there would often be a question of whether it could find the dedicated server on each PC, or whether I'd have to go futzing around in the network settings—not an easy thing to do when you're 13 and stupid.
Nonetheless, there were quite a few games that made it all the way through the gauntlet. The one I remember most vividly is Half-Life: Opposing Force deathmatch—which was basically Half-Life deathmatch with more maps and more weapons. One of OpFor's multiplayer maps, Datacore , was the perfect size for three players, and we'd spend hours setting up laser traps for one another around the map's tight, electric-blue corridors. Another favourite was Paradox Park , which we spent ages in despite the fact it was impractically large for three players.
Pragmatism influenced what we played a lot. While my brother and I never struggled to fill that third chair (weirdly, it isn't hard to get other kids to come around to your house when you have a LAN in your attic), three players was a challenging number with a lot of game

pool.titulo: While you wait for The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel, you owe it to yourself to play Tainted Grail
pool.resumen: They do make them like they used to.
pool.contenido:
Dungeon Master Welcome to Dungeon Master , PC Gamer's regular RPG column, where Online Editor Fraser Brown delves into PC gaming's most beloved and enduring genre. Grab a seat in our badly-lit tavern and please ignore the goblin puke.
I will probably be in the ground when Bethesda finally releases The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel —which is kind of liberating. I have hype immunity. But what's even more liberating is the fact that there's already an RPG that does everything I want from an Elder Scrolls game—2025's Tainted Grail: The Fall of Avelon.
Tainted Grail is unabashedly created in the mould of The Elder Scrolls, in that it is a primarily first-person fantasy RPG where flexibility is its superpower. You chart your own course and effectively construct your class, enhancing skills by using them as much as possible. But it is not merely the Elder Scrolls we have at home—it captures the very best that this kind of RPG can offer, and in some ways manages to outdo Bethesda.
This is apparent right from the get-go. In classic Elder Scrolls form, Tainted Grail begins with you banged up in a facility that incarcerates and studies unfortunates afflicted with a magical plague, of which you are one. Follow the critical path and you will meet a new friend, get in some tough fights and then escape.
By the time I finally escaped the island and began my adventure proper, I already knew this RPG was special.
But this island asylum is big. Really big. It's full of locked doors, hidden rooms, large spaces ripe for some big brawls, a subterranean area waiting to be delved into, oodles of lore—there are hours of rooting around to be done. So I ignored the critical path, had a big old wander, and by the time I finally escaped the island and began my adventure proper, I already knew this RPG was special.
While Tainted Grail is full of bespoke quests sending you off into the open world on countless adventures, these are really just designed to get you out the door so you can stumble upon something cool—a new enemy that will utterly destroy you, a powerful weapon hidden in a crypt, an eccentric immortal being who wants to make a deal. The vibe is very TTRPG, which isn't surprising, given that it's based on one.
And these adventures are actually dangerous. Deadly, even. The villains of Tainted Grail hit hard, and early on you will feel horrifyingly vulnerable. Basic bandits and skeletons can easily spell your doom. And if you stay out at night, you're screwed. Avelon is a miserable, cruel place, cursed and plagued, and you will struggle.
Developer Questline didn't simply up the lethality and call it a day, though. Tainted Grail, unlike The Elder Scrolls, actually has a quality combat system that falls firmly into the skill-based category. It's no Dark Souls, but it's more Dark Souls than Skyrim. So that increased level of challenge feels earned because of the tools you have available to you, and the range of combat styles you can develop.
With all the options you have at your disposal—which has been further enhanced by DLC additions, letting you, for example, go through this Arthurian fantasy RPG as a kung-fu master—it can be hard to commit to a build. I've been spellblading it up, with my alchemical skills helping to shore up my weaknesses, but every time I encounter a new piece of gear I wonder what else I could create. But you do need to commit eventually. This isn't a game for a jack of all trades.
While Bethesda is more deft at crafting believable, reactive lands, Tainted Grail's world design also deserves its flowers. It's a smaller space, divided into three main areas, and while you can absolutely muck around for hundreds of hours, you can experience most of what it has to offer in 50. But what you'll experience in those 50 hours is so much more meticulously designed, with Questline getting so much out of each location.
It's a game full of aesthetic juxtapositions.
It's a looker, too. What it lacks in fidelity it more than makes up for in the art design department, and it's another place where Dark Souls rears its gorgeously hideous head. Tainted Grail finds beauty in the grim misery of its fantastical post-apocalyptic realm. It's a game full of aesthetic juxtapositions—the arboreal and the horrific, the grounded and alien. Avelon is delightfully strange, and that makes exploration all the more thrilling.
As games grow ever larger and more bloated, my appreciation for richer, better-scoped worlds like Avalon only grows. And this does not indicate a dearth of ambition on Questline's part. Tainted Grail is a complex, elaborate game that will happily devour your days and keep showing you new things.
Clearly people want this—Tainted Grail has done very well for itself, garnering more than 20,000 user reviews on Steam , where its rating sits at Very Positive. It's a reassuring reminder that you do not need a gargantuan studio and big publisher money to make a quality RPG in the Elder Scrolls style.
We don't know how many people are working on Sentinel right now, but we can expect the number to be large. Skyrim had around 100 people working on it, and with Starfield that jumped to more than 400. Tainted Grail was made by 50 people. That's quite the achievement.
So if you're craving a side-quest-heavy sandbox RPG with plenty of sword fights and spellflinging, Tainted Grail should absolutely be your next port of call. And the good news is that there's a demo . No excuses. Go play it.

pool.titulo: Seven years on since Persona 5 Royal, Atlus says 'people won't have to wait as long as they have previously' for the next game after Persona 6
pool.resumen: "Persona 6 is not the end".
pool.contenido:
The amount of time it takes to develop games has been growing steadily longer for decades, and Atlus' Persona series is no exception to this rule. While Persona 4 Golden and Persona 5 were separated by four years (long considered standard for game development) it's been seven years since Persona 5 Royal and Persona 6 still doesn’t have a release date—though we did get Metaphor: ReFantazio in between.
Nonetheless, it's an issue that P-Studio is very much aware of, and it was recently addressed by general producer Kazuhisa Wada. In an interview with Sega Samania (via Eurogamer ) Wada stressed that the wait for whatever comes after Persona 6 will be shorter.
"Persona 6 is not the end," Wada explained. "We have been working to make sure that people won't have to wait as long for the next game as they have previously. In order for Persona to grow as an IP, we consider how to live up to people's expectations in terms of creativity and development every day."
Now, we're probably not looking at a dramatic reduction in development time. Wada emphasised that "large-scale RPGs like the Personal series can take five years or more to develop," adding that. "There can be a long time between numbered entries." Yet even if the average timeline was five years, that would be a considerable improvement.
Wada doesn't explain how Atlus plans to speed up development of its games. But there's always one question when developers begin talking about making games quicker—does it involve generative AI? Wada expressed interest in the tech several years ago, stating that it might be useful for "early concept and idea formation" and that the Atlus art team had been "talking about wanting to implement AI." That said, there's been little, if any talk about AI from Atlus since, and there's no evidence at present that Persona 6 uses the tech.
In fact, Atlus hasn't said much about Persona 6 at all since the game was announced earlier this year, though there are rumours that we'll find out more at The Game Awards in a few weeks' time. As for Wada, while he didn't comment on Persona 6 in detail, he did say that Atlus is "creating something better than anything we've made before, and that is hugely satisfying."

pool.titulo: Deltarune chapter 6 is 'structurally complete' while development has begun on chapter 7, according to Toby Fox
pool.resumen: "All the maps, events and battles exist" for the next slice of the RPG.
pool.contenido:
Eight years on since the launch of its first chapter, Deltarune seems to be rapidly approaching completion. With five chapters already released for Toby Fox's sequel to the beloved RPG Undertale , two more are expected before the game is complete. And according to Deltarune creator Toby Box, not only is chapter 6 close to being finished, but work has also already begun on chapter 7.
Fox provided the status update in his most recent newsletter . Kicking off with a general note that chapter 6 is "progressing well", Fox explains that "the game is now a structurally complete draft that can be played from the beginning to the end. He further elaborates that "all the maps, events and battles exist", with the exception of one optional event that's still being worked on.
As a result, the Deltarune team is now at the point where they feel comfortable commencing localisation and preliminary testing. Fox clarifies, however, that full testing won't begin just yet, as "some important scenes and details are still undercooked in their presentation". Indeed, while chapter 6 is progressing rapidly, players shouldn't expect an imminent release. "Even though chapter 6 is a rather short chapter, I would like it to be as good as possible. I won't be able to rush this," Fox points out.
As for Chapter 7, Fox says that development has "only just started". Designers who have finished their Chapter 6 work have moved on to work on the new chapter, while Fox has shared some of the dialogue and events with the Deltarune team. "Just when the story reached a critical moment, I stopped reading. I told my team they need to complete more of the game before I tell them what happens," he explained, adding that "Everyone agrees it's more fun this way."
It's impressive progress, considering that chapter 5 released in June. Then again, development of Deltarune has accelerated rapidly since 2025, when Fox released chapters 3 and 4 of the game in the same year. The launch of chapter 5 also demonstrated just how much fans want to see the story through, as 300,000 concurrent players flocked to Steam to check out the latest chunk of the game.

pool.titulo: Expedition 33 lead writer says Grand Theft Auto 6 layoff concerns show that 'people creating the value do not receive a proportionate amount of that value'
pool.resumen: "I sincerely hope the Rockstar team is successful in unionizing".
pool.contenido:
Grand Theft Auto 6 is already enormously successful, having enjoyed "the biggest entertainment launch in history" . But the current games industry is such that some Rockstar developers are still concerned about being laid off in the wake of its release. Writing for the Guardian prior to GTA 6's launch, Rockstar animation programmer Nestor Uriarte explained that although there is "no indication that layoffs are coming" it nonetheless "says a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off."
It might sound odd for the developers of such a hugely successful game to be worried about losing their jobs, but layoffs don't just occur when games or companies struggle commercially. A common cause of layoffs in the games industry is companies trying to reduce overheads after a game has launched, as the studio switches from full production to post-release support for their current game and planning for the next one.
It's partly why the industry seems to be in a constant, rolling state of layoffs, even when games appear to sell well. This issue was recently addressed by Jennifer Svedberg-Yen, the lead writer of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 . Svedberg-Yen, who left Sandfall Interactive in July , claimed that the problem is exacerbated by an imbalance in who benefits financially when a game like Grand Theft Auto 6 launches.
"99 Metacritic score. Multiple award nominations before it even released. Massive sales and player engagement. Incredible amounts of tangible and intangible value creation. Yet the team is worried about layoffs," Svedberg-Yen wrote in an Instagram post. "So, who receives the lion's share of the profits from their labor? Not the vast majority of the creative team."
Svedberg-Yen pointed out that this is "one of the issues that happens when the people creating the value do not receive a proportionate amount of that value," adding that "In finance, we call that value extraction."
Svedberg-Yen also commented on the Rockstar team's ongoing efforts to unionise, with the team in the process of voting on whether or not it wants a union. If successful, the Rockstar Game Workers Union would become the biggest in the UK's gaming sector.
"I sincerely hope the Rockstar team is successful in unionizing," Svedberg-Yen wrote. "Layoffs during lulls in development cycles would work a lot better if teams were properly paid for the value they create, not just one-time, but throughout the life of the thing they created."
The games industry has seen a huge number of layoffs in the last few years. A recent report by GDC found that 34% of developers it surveyed had been laid off since 2024. Xbox alone has cut thousands of jobs , with more planned going into January 2027. Most recently, Firaxis, owned by GTA 6 publisher Take Two Interactive, reportedly laid off a third of its staff earlier this week as it works on a new XCOM.

pool.titulo: In GTA 6, Cars Are Way, Way More Than Just Getaway Wheels
pool.resumen: GTA has always been obsessed with cars, but in GTA 6 your wheels are for more than just getaways - they're your mobile base.
pool.contenido:
The clue's in the name: Grand Theft Auto is a series obsessed with cars. Stealing them, racing them, modding them, escaping the police in them, bopping your head to their iconic radio stations, and sitting in the passenger seat conversing with colourful NPCs as you drive between missions.
But even in this petrolheaded company, GTA 6 stands out.
I'm not talking about the sheer variety of vehicles , from mobility scooters to muscle cars, nor the distinct grunts of its engines and whirr of superchargers, or even its expanded customization that tweaks everything from the upholstery to the transmission. It goes way beyond that: in GTA 6, your car is a mobile base, an extension of your character that sits at the centre of GTA's revamped and reworked systems. Without a car – specifically, without an owned car, rather than one nicked from the side of the street – I'm naked.
First, your car is the only way to manage all the guns you'll need.
In GTA 6, you physically carry weapons rather than hiding them in magically deep pockets. You can only wield two "longarms" – think rifles and shotguns – at a time, one on your back and one in a hand, and realistically you'll only want to carry one at a time because double-parking guns makes the no-nonsense cops twitchy.
Thankfully the trunk of your car can carry extra weapons (sneaking up to cop cars and jimmying the boot can get you a fresh gun in a pinch). Owned vehicles carry all your purchased weapons at once and you can switch them at will. Whenever I'm planning anything remotely violent, such as the lucrative gang hideout robberies, I take my owned vehicle so I'm prepared for anything.
I want to properly invest in my cars. In upgrades, yes, but also in mastering the act of driving them, learning their nuances and quirks. Second, cars hold stashes of pilfered contraband.
Drugs, marked bills, jewellery: anything you steal worth a damn in GTA 6 is stuffed in a bag slung across your shoulder, and selling it through fences is a reliable way to accrue cash. Like with guns, you can only carry as many bags as you have arms. Your car becomes your pack mule, able to stack several stash bags at once so you can steal in sprees, rather than having to sell after every job.
Again, your owned vehicle is better because it'll retain your stash bags indefinitely, and between sessions. You can hit a drug den, head home to sleep, finish a few missions, quit the game, boot it up again hours later and your stash bag will still be safe. Even if you're busted, you should still be able to retrieve your personal wheels from the impound (and you absolutely should: sneaking into impounds is one of GTA 6's most satisfying activities).
Third, and arguably the most important: your car is a mobile wardrobe that can hold five outfits plus extra hats.
That's more crucial than it sounds because of how the police work in GTA 6. When you're clocked as a criminal, cops will have your description, but a new outfit, hat and sunglasses completely covers the scent of sin. You could buy some new clothes, of course, but you'll need a nearby clothes shop and some cash. It's easier and faster to grab some new gear from your trunk and drive off like nothing happened.
These three factors mean that when I have to dump my owned vehicle – changing cars to lose the police, for example – I feel vulnerable. Thankfully, it's easy to get it back by calling Joey in Chapter 1, or via the ScooterBros app, which you unlock later.
All these systems make me want to properly invest in my cars. In upgrades, yes, but also in mastering the act of driving them, learning their nuances and quirks. In GTA 5, Franklin's Bravado Buffalo S was just another vehicle to me, and I was constantly swapping between stolen cars to get from A to B, each handling differently. In GTA 6, I know exactly how much throttle Jason's Ganado pickup can take before it tailslides, and exactly the right angle for skidding around swampy corners without wrapping around a tendrilled tree.
And I take more care when weaving through traffic because crashing in GTA 6 peels off fenders and crumples bumpers faster than ever.
The Official GTA 6 Guide, Only on IGN Just getting started in GTA 6 or wondering what to do next? Check out the Official Grand Theft Auto 6 guide right here on IGN. If you're still getting your bearings, discover GTA's new systems with the Beginner's Guide - 67 Tips and Tricks , or get all the details on the first chapters with the Chapter 1 Guide and Tips and Chapter 2 Guide and Tips . If you're already driving all around Leonida and want to know everything there is to find and do, see the Leonida interactive map .
I'm deep into Chapter 2, but (mild spoiler alert!) I haven't even begun registering and storing new cars in garages. I've stolen and sold plenty – another new feature in GTA 6 – and will steal and sell plenty more. No doubt GTA 6's preoccupation with vehicles will continue, and I can't wait to see how cars change as the game unfolds.
If Red Dead Redemption 2 is the horse game, shrunken bollocks and all, then GTA 6 is without doubt the car game.

pool.titulo: The Binding of Isaac Dev Removes Undisclosed AI-Generated Music From Repentance+ Following Creator Response, Review-Bombing
pool.resumen: The Binding of Isaac developer Nicalis has removed undisclosed AI-generated music included in Repentance+ after backlash led to a review-bombing campaign on Steam and a response from the game's creator, Edmund McMillen.
pool.contenido:
The Binding of Isaac developer Nicalis has removed undisclosed AI-generated music included in Repentance+ after backlash led to a review-bombing campaign on Steam and a response from the game's creator, Edmund McMillen.
McMillen and Nicalis spent months building up to the November 19, 2026, release date for the latest update in their classic action roguelike game, but that launch was quickly soured. Just 8% of The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+'s recent Steam reviews are positive, with a good chunk of comments left by players referencing AI-generated material that was not previously mentioned in any official capacity.
"Thanks, Nicalis, for breaking everything and adding AI slop to an already-existing game!" one popular review said .
"I'm starting to think that adding AI to a game should be valid grounds to refunds to people who have already paid for and played a game," another said . "Shameful they would do this to an Indie gem. Shameful."
The allegedly AI-generated content in question seems to be music exclusively tied to a specific, Grand Theft Auto-themed run meant to coincide with the recent release of GTA 6 . What could have been a cute jab at another gaming titan boiled into a full-blown controversy for Nicalis when Reddit user ShweetsStuff reported the questionable tunes just one day after launch.
As artificial intelligence advances, it's become increasingly difficult to discern human-made art from content pushed out by machines, but ShweetsStuff was able to provide evidence backing their claims. Specifically, they pointed to a handful of tracks that mention AI music software Suno in their metadata, which also included links to their Suno pages.
Rep+'s GTAVI run's music is 100% generated by Suno (AI) (with proof)
by
u/ShweetsStuff in
bindingofisaac
AI-generated content passed off as art has already become controversial on its own in recent years. Adding to the fire for The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ was the fact that the music was featured in the new update without any sort of update to its Steam description. Valve requires developers to disclose how they may have used AI during game development, making the music's inclusion as puzzling as it is concerning for those who felt Nicalis had pulled the wool over their eyes.
Negative reviews poured in following ShweetsStuff's discovery, leading McMillen to issue a statement today. He said he “had no idea" how AI-generated music found its way into the launch build of The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+'s new update.
"Woke up to a s**t show," he said , "obviously I had no idea it featured generated music in the daily run, looking into how that happened and getting it removed, stay tuned."
Please report issues and bugs to the email attached.
— 🜏 Edmund McMillen 🜏 (@edmundmcmillen) November 21, 2026
Just hours later, Nicalis launched a new patch, confirming the "removal of generated music files." The update is currently live for PC, with the studio adding that it has already been submitted to Microsoft, Nintendo, and Sony. When exactly it will go live for those platforms remains to be seen.
No explanation for how or why the AI-generated music was included was provided. Instead, the team simply said it was "working on the game and will continue to address new and old bugs." McMillen also encouraged fans to report issues and bugs to the developers.
In the meantime, The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+'s recent reviews on Steam remain firmly in the "Overwhelmingly Negative" category. The major update also coincided with the launch of Repentance+ on new platforms, including Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S. pool.contenido:
GTA 6 players on PlayStation 5 have reported frequent crashes tied to error code CE-108255-1, and it looks like it's blocking them from progressing through the story while they wait for Sony and Rockstar to send out a fix.
Although Rockstar Games spent a decade making its new Grand Theft Auto game, it's no surprise to see the new highest-rated game of all time launching with at least a few hiccups. Some have it worse than others, though, with more than a few reports of crashes affecting PS5 consoles popping up online in the days following GTA 6's launch.
The most common cause seems to be tied to error code CE-108255-1, which, as defined by Sony , simply indicates that "an error occurred with the game/application." It seems that, although the majority of players aren't encountering the issue, those who have haven't been able to find a proper fix. Adding to the trouble is that those who have met these dreaded GTA 6 crashes are getting them pretty frequently, and what's triggering them isn't always clear. There are reports from players on both standard PS5 and PS5 Pro consoles running into these issues, with some even saying that crashes appear to be tied to the story, barring them from making any progress.
GTA 6 keeps crashing with error code CE-108255-1 on PS5 soon as I use plunger during Pipework mission – tried almost everything, still no fix
by
u/Acrobatic-Promise458 in
PS5HelpSupport
"I've noticed that the issue manifests differently for different players," one Reddit user said . "In my case, the game crashes on Jason's loading screen: it freezes and then displays the CE-108255-1 error code, meaning I can't even get into the game. Others manage to play for a few minutes before experiencing a crash. I really hope Sony and Rockstar work together to investigate and resolve this issue as soon as possible."
Game crashes are annoying for anyone, but when a massive game like GTA 6, which many feel has a less-than-generous autosave system , suddenly boots players back to the PS5 home screen without warning, it can be especially troublesome. Many who have reported the crashes to PlayStation Support say they've been directed to Rockstar, while those who report to Rockstar say they're being directed to PlayStation. One player said they feel like they're "stuck in an endless support loop, with a game I paid for and still can't play."
Meanwhile, those who have managed to get help say most assistance hasn't been able to completely resolve their issues. However, some have said they've had luck with a few tried-and-true methods, such as uninstalling and reinstalling the game, making sure both the PS5 and game have their most recent updates, and restoring licenses.
"I’ve done everything possible to solve this," another player said . "Deleted cache. Rebuilt database, deleted everything else from my console, took it apart, cleaned it, turned HDR off, switched to 1080p, went and updated game license, deleted and reinstalled and still crashing. Ugh. I’ve got a day 1 PS5 with a disc drive. Other friends of mine with the same console are playing with no issue."
Again, it's unclear if the crashing issue is tied specifically to the PS5 or GTA 6 itself. Until either entity comes up with an update, though, all affected players are stuck on launch weekend.
GTA 6 released for PS5 and Xbox Series X/S November 19 and, in its first 24 hours, made Rockstar $3.79 billion. pool.titulo: Blade Director Says He Walked Away From Marvel's Canceled Movie Because 'Life's Too Short to Make S**t Films'
pool.resumen: Director Bassam Tariq has opened up about why he exited Marvel's Blade movie, saying, "life's too short to make s**t films."
pool.contenido:
Director Bassam Tariq has opened up about why he exited Marvel's Blade movie, saying, "life's too short to make s**t films."
The Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother filmmaker explained his reasoning for walking away from the Mahershala Ali superhero period piece during an interview with The New Arab . With just one other feature film (Mogul Mowgli) under his belt at the time, working on Blade presented quite the opportunity, but his short time attached as the flick's first director wound up being more of a learning lesson than anything else.
"It was funny and strange to start casting and building without a proper script," Tariq said when asked what working in the studio system taught him. "You're sitting there and explaining to actors what their role will be, and they just have to believe you.
"That's also very dangerous because if the text comes and it doesn't add up to what you were saying, your credibility gets completely shot. All I have is my integrity, and I've been thinking about that a lot."
Marvel Studios announced an Ali-led Blade film in 2019 and picked Tariq to lead the charge in 2021. A little more than one year later, and the director was said to have bounced off the project , with Marvel telling The Hollywood Reporter that "shifts in our production schedule" were to blame.
Today, one new director and multiple frustrated Ali updates later, and Blade has been finally, officially canceled . Marvel Cinematic Universe orchestrator Kevin Feige said the process made him feel like a "gigantic loser and failure" – an assessment Ali agreed with – but for Tariq, the decision to cut off his relationship with Blade came down to how it was impacting his relationship with the film's actors. He told The New Arab that being "the bearer of bad news to your actors" while a corporate entity makes all of the major decisions in the background is "not a great way to be a director."
"I know some people can take that and run with it, but I learned I was losing credibility with my actors, and it wasn't a healthy way to operate as a filmmaker. Life's too short to make s**t films, so that was my big lesson: I have to have full control over my script. If we disagree, it's between them and me. It's quite sad because we had such high hopes for what we wanted to build."
For now, as Marvel heads into another major release with next month's Avengers: Doomsday, there seems to be no sign of a live-action Blade for the MCU. Although the process of trying to get the movie out the door seems to have been tumultuous behind the scenes, there doesn't seem to be any bad blood from Tariq. In fact, when talking about how exiting the film made him feel like a failure last month, the director defended Feige, calling him a "good dude."
Although Ali's Blade never came to be, some of the effort put into the film did eventually see daylight. The actor went on to thank Marvel for the free year of physical training he got, which wound up helping him during the more intense scenes in Tariq's Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother. Costumes from Blade were also famously used in Ryan Coogler's Sinners .

pool.titulo: GTA 6’s Weirdest Cow Shows Why You Should Pause the Story Early To Explore Its Vast Map
pool.resumen: I escaped GTA 6's starting neighborhood to explore the wider world, and you'll never believe what happened with this cow I found.
pool.contenido:
Warning: this story features spoilers for an optional side activity.
"Save me."
Those two chilling words were so soft I wondered if I'd heard them correctly – after all, the only souls in this orchard were me and Tootsie, an escaped cow draped in red cloth with a rosette stuck to her forehead.
But no, I had heard them, and I turned them over in my head as I led Tootsie back along her rampaging path, through fallen fruit, over a busted wooden fence, and to her owner, a dairy farmer I'd found on the side of the road, flustered and crying about his prized $2 million show cow.
I was still processing those two words as we approached the farmer's trailer, and when he told me that tonight, a fan had paid to watch a private Tootsie mud bath, I knew what I had to do. I shooed her to her freedom – "Go, run! Live your best life!" – and she galloped, ribbons fluttering, hooves pounding into the distance. To freedom rather than a busy highway, I hoped.
I was Jason, the good Samaritan (if you ignore the part where I then provoked the farmer to start a fight, knocked him out cold, stamped on his limp body and stole the $500 in his pocket).
This was about six hours into Rockstar's latest masterpiece . For a game as vast and open as GTA 6 , I found the opening strangely claustrophobic – to begin, the giant map of Leonida is shrouded in fog apart from the sliver of the Florida Keys where Jason lives and some surrounding swamp land. Key Lento is so dense with activities, shops, missions, and random encounters, not to mention the constant distraction of pottering around Jason's waterside house, that I felt overwhelmed by it all. And so, perhaps earlier than the game wanted me to, I pointed Jason's red pickup north and started driving.
What I found was that GTA 6's open world holds delights that you can enjoy no matter where you are in the main story.
I slipped west of Vice City, turning off the highway's spiralling spaghetti junctions near Buckskin Swamp. Soon I parked up at Emerald Springs, a nature reserve with pristine boardwalks and stands selling orange juice and doughnuts. I plodded the planks, eating a sandwich from the Black Bear Deli. I studied some ducks, beat up an entitled British tourist, stole a bike, and pedalled back to my car.
Every scripted random encounter so far has felt deliciously crafted. Some funny, some nightmarish. I had hoped to find something crafted and scripted, but the fact that I could still have fun in a place with ostensibly nothing to do fills me with hope for the rest of the game. It was stark how, in just a few minutes of driving from Key Lento, the atmosphere had shifted completely, from road rage to tranquility. The beauty of the place and the amusing conversations to eavesdrop were captivating, even without a weird or wonderful encounter.
That came soon enough.
I placed another waypoint vaguely northeast. It was on the way that I met Tootsie for what was undoubtedly the strangest moment I've had so far in GTA 6. Not only did it imply that animals could talk in this world, or at least psychically communicate, but that Jason could hear them. I wonder if that means anything.
My detour from the main story had been worth it for Tootise (and the $500 from her owner) but it was barely lunchtime. GTA 6's extended day-night cycle feels central to how you play: you can get so much more done in a day than in Red Dead Redemption 2, and even after a languid morning routine of working out and coffee, you're still out the door before 08:00am.
Low on gas, I rolled into a forecourt in Ambrosia, a town where abandoned factories and containers made way for quaint high streets. I was rewarded with another unique scene. A chap with a camo shirt and teeth like a Donegal graveyard spraying gasoline into a bathtub inexplicably mounted in the back of his pickup.
"None of your regulations or mind control is going to stop me!" he shouted as the liquid sloshed down his tailgate, coating the dozen bumper stickers and dripping onto his boots. "I can pump gasoline wherever I want."
He even sprayed it on Jason, and it took the threat of nearby sirens to hold me back. Thankfully, his cigarette did the work instead, falling and lighting the gas on fire, the flames engulfing his feet. "Those cigarettes'll kill ya man," Jason said, smirking.
Every scripted random encounter so far has felt deliciously crafted. Some funny, some nightmarish. I like that they vary in length and level of interactivity so that when one starts, you never know if it'll trigger an actual quest or just puff into nothingness. I could've just watched the gas station spectacle unfold, like a mini stage play, but hours later when I found a tiger mauling bodies in an abandoned swamp hotel, I had to act.
Later, I ambled a row of cafes and restaurants, got a haircut, ate a protein bar, and threw the protein bar wrapper at a guy who looked at me funny, sparking a seven-person brawl that drew the attention of a cops and – when I gunned one officer down – a police chopper.
Chapter 1 encourages you to stay local, but you don't need to wait until the story nudges you north. I was forced to flee even further north, driving along some railtracks and into the wilderness, not able to stop at the wonderfully named Thrillbully Mud Club. I eventually lost the police chopper and looped back to Ambrosia as the sun dawdled. I wanted to get back by bedtime but I didn't fancy the seven-mile drive back to Key Lento, and as if Rockstar was reading my thoughts, the next corner I rounded revealed a hospital complete with a helipad. I climbed into the cockpit, apologising silently to the next poor sod who needed airlifting to safety, and flew south.
I could have seen this all later in the game.
