pool.titulo: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping Ending Explained and the Cardinal Sin of Prequels
pool.resumen: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping ending explained: We take a look at the latest entry in the franchise and examine the cardinal sin of prequels.
pool.contenido:
Spoilers for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping follow.
When we first meet him in The Hunger Games, Haymitch Abernathy (originally portrayed by Woody Harrelson) is a broken, bitter, cynical alcoholic deeply uninterested in — or perhaps incapable of — helping Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson) survive the Games: his one job. Throughout the four original films, he transforms into a man who is not only trustworthy but who plays an integral role in the plan to finally, definitively, take down the Capitol. It’s one of the more powerful arcs in the series, one that speaks to the power of Katniss’ ability — mostly unwillingly and unwittingly —to inspire hope. The end of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the beginning of the Haymitch we have known; the issue is that the additions in this new film detract from the character rather than enrich him.
How Sunrise on the Reaping Ends While the Haymitch of Sunrise on the Reaping (beautifully portrayed by Joseph Zada) is technically victorious in his Games, he has brutally lost to the Capitol and President Snow (Ralph Fiennes). As Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin) reviews Haymitch’s gameplay for a (presumably) Panem-wide audience, it is clear that the Gamemakers have edited Haymitch’s footage to show him in the worst possible light. From the Capitol’s perspective, he’s an ideal victor: unfeeling, ruthless, self-serving, cowardly, and lacking regard for the other tributes. This image of Haymitch is designed by the Capitol to serve its purpose; to make people selfish is to keep them separate and incapable of effectively challenging power. The intent is to send Haymitch home a pariah rather than a conquering hero who inspires others in 12 to reach beyond their current position. It also plays on his very real shame for failing to “break the Games,” which — as the Capitol did in the arena — forces him into isolation. Manipulating the footage is a tactic that, as we’ll get to, creates a real problem for the original films.
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping Review
When Haymitch returns to 12, the Capitol has timed it so that he arrives just in time to watch his family burn alive in their small home, but too late to save them. With added cruelty, Snow allows him to briefly believe that the love of his life, Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak), will be spared, only for her to die from Snow’s poison, hidden in what looks like the candy Haymitch so lovingly gave her at the start of the film. The metaphor is clear: All the sweetness in his life has been irrevocably poisoned. He is left terrified that the Capitol will murder anyone he is close to, so he keeps everyone at bay. Early in the film, Haymitch made it clear he wanted no part of winning, or the lonely, traumatized, lifeless survival it would mean; Snow’s ultimate punishment is forcing him to live exactly that fate.
Snow, however, was manipulated into sparing Haymitch by Jesse Plemons’ Plutarch Heavensbee, who is playing the looooong game and wants to keep Haymitch around as a potential ally to one day end the Capitol’s authoritarian reign of terror. Plutarch knew Haymitch’s loved ones would likely be taken from him; he suggested as much. But he valued a future strategic alliance more than Haymitch’s peace. (With friends like these…) Ultimately, the Games portrayed in this film act as a dress rehearsal for Catching Fire’s conspiracy to “break the Games,” which is in part the issue with this story; more on that in a bit.

The first is Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), one of District 12’s two female tributes. She’s basically a walking middle finger to the Games and the Capitol. The second is his murdered love, Lenore, who introduced the film’s central recurring theme, “nothing is inevitable,” meaning don’t submit to a fate you don’t want just because the current system wants you to believe there’s nothing you can do about it.
As images of Haymitch — angry, drunk, alone, and at odds with the community (in one shot, he is literally walking in the opposite direction) — play out on screen, he swears to be a terrible victor, to be disruptive, and presumably to eventually do what he set out to do in this film: end the Games. After being the teetotaling light of the community earlier in the film, he has become the Haymitch we know, even lurking behind a tree as his former friends cradle their new baby girl, little Katniss Everdeen. Throughout the series of images, he stands grimly before caskets as body after body is sent back to 12 from the Games. Believing he is too dangerous to be around, he lets no one comfort him.
Turning the original Hunger Games story into the fulfillment of Haymitch’s long-delayed goal undercuts the power of those first films. The film concludes with a very brief flash-forward in which Lawrence, Hutcherson, and Harrelson return as the grown Katniss, Peeta, and an older Haymitch, celebrating that there is no more Reaping (which had taken place each year on Haymitch’s birthday). They thank one another for what they each did to end the bloodshed; then Haymitch goes to sit on the hill where he once found refuge with Lenore.
One is led to believe that Haymitch is at peace. Lenore promised that change is possible, and Plutarch assured Haymitch that each act of rebellion adds a spark that may lead to the next, and that even if they never see the results in their lifetime, the effort is worth it. pool.titulo: How Rockstar Made Every NPC Feel Alive in GTA 6
pool.resumen: Rockstar made NPCs feel alive in GTA 6 by "establishing deep backstories for almost everything" throughout Leonida.
pool.contenido:
Game developers often refer to their open world cities as characters due to the sheer craftsmanship involved in building out a believable, diverse playspace for the player with its own districts, history, and architecture. This is truer for GTA 6 than most games, but what makes Leonida really feel alive — outside of the puddles of bin juice, the regional-specific cop cars, and mapped out power grid — are the people who live there.
GTA 6 feels like a massive evolution in what it means to be a non-player character (NPC) because there’s an emphasis on the “C” — they’re actually characters in their own right. NPCs don’t just all look unique — with body types, skin, dress style, and hair making them stand apart — they have their own personalities and temperaments. Start a fight with one NPC and they might fight back, while another runs away. One could start a fight by slapping you, another might flick their cigarette at you or tip their drink over your head. Passersby can cheer the fight on, flee, or get involved. Some stop after a single punch knocks sense into them, while others swing until they’re out cold .
No matter where you go in GTA 6, it feels like a lived-in world, on the macro and micro scale. There are over 100 interiors to explore, and each house tells you a story about its occupants. Listen to conversations out on the streets and you’ll get a window into their minds, built out by an entire Rockstar studio dedicated to making them authentic and believable, while still being larger-than-life, funny, and often unhinged.
“A big part of it was establishing deep backstories for almost everything, even if they were never meant to be fully explained to the player, and then really sticking to those backstories,” said Steven Messinger, Rockstar's senior design director for the open world. “For example, our gang compounds have a complex drug network we’ve fully mapped out: where the drugs come from, who brings them in and how, how they’re distributed to each compound, what happens at each stop, and how they eventually reach the street-level buyer.
“Players will only pick up on bits and pieces of this, but having that structure in the background as something we consistently refer to helps everything feel more real, like this big machine is always running even when players aren’t there.”
To build this tangible sense of place, Rockstar takes in-depth research trips for GTA games , embedding the writers in the mundane and the more extreme to really capture the soul of a city. Helicopter trips of the Florida Keys, ride-alongs with police, talking to people, taking photos and notes, all build up a snapshot that Rockstar bottles up to digitize in video game format.
“We had a lot of fun trying to capture the raw energy and vibrant chaos that Florida is known for,” said senior design director of world and population, John Macpherson. “By immersing ourselves into a number of these locations on reference trips, spending time with locals, experiencing as much as possible firsthand, we gathered a direct sense of what would make Leonida feel truly alive.
“Everywhere you look, little stories constantly unfold. It could be as simple as what someone’s wearing, how fit they are, how they walk and talk, who they’re with, what tunes they’re blasting as they cruise down the street. We tried to match that in-game as much as possible, hopefully resulting in something that feels full of life.”
You can walk along Vice Beach and see sugar daddies with their trophy wives, locals playing volleyball, tourists sunbathing, and people walking their pets. Everywhere you look, there’s something happening in Leonida, and it’s completely enveloping. You feel like a part of its world, rather than a godlike being with total control over it.
There’s a mission around the midpoint of the game where protagonists Jason and Lucia people-watch from a hotel sunbed, inventing backstories for the guests by the pool, and it’s something I found myself doing as I explored the world and passed people by, such is the variety and diversity of the game’s NPCs. No other game has ever had such a colorful cast of extras, which is wild when you consider all this was built to add credibility to a world you can zoom past at 100mph.
“We evolved from monolithic NPCs built to visual standards that were lower than the main cast in GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2, to fully fleshed-out characters with singular awareness and visual identities,” said Valmor Garcia, senior technical art director on GTA 6. “They are driven by dynamic moods, personalities, unique anatomy, facial features, and dialogue that are visually on par with our protagonists, Jason and Lucia.”
Rockstar built entirely new technology for GTA 6 to simulate hair, cloth, and the way muscles move under the skin. All that work is implemented equally across all characters, so there’s never that uncanny moment where you come face-to-face with a flat and lifeless NPC, staring at you with dead eyes. Everyone you meet is equally detailed, and the range of visual design is staggering.
Of course, this approach created challenges in other areas of development. It’s fairly straightforward to implement a combat system in a game where all character models are approximately the same size, but the varied body types of GTA 6 meant Rockstar had to take a look at how it approached animations so physical contact looks good no matter how big or small the character models are. Especially since this is a game where the two leads can also change in size through diet and exercise .

pool.titulo: This '90s-inspired horror game has one of the coolest post-apocalyptic worlds I've ever seen
pool.resumen: Plus you can experience it all from the comfort of your campervan.
pool.contenido:
I often find myself thinking where the best place to survive a zombie apocalypse would be. A walled-off stone house would certainly make for some good defenses, a boat would be great—but only if the zombies didn't pull a Fear the Walking Dead—or you could spend the end of the world in a camper van. That would certainly be whimsical.
You do just this in The Road of Dust and Sorrow's demo , although it's certainly not as whimsical as I first imagined it to be. You see, in this 2D horror game you have bigger responsibilities than just keeping yourself alive, you also have a young daughter to look out for as well.
This isn't an easy task. Supplies are dwindling, zombie-like humans infected by addictive chemicals amble across the land in search of more dust, but they'll settle for your blood instead. Plus there's this creepy Pastor who's definitely up to something very bad. I only got one glimpse of him in the demo and he was surrounded by a lot of gore and eldritch horror, so I've just decided that staying away from him is probably for the best.
But you can't hunker down and forget about all these terrors, because you have a daughter to feed and protect. So I spent most of my time in the demo gathering food, medical supplies, and trying to locate an item that may just grant us safe passage to the only sanctuary humanity has left.
The dev, Painted Black Games, says it took inspiration from horror series like Silent Hill and Resident Evil for The Road of Dust and Sorrow, and while I haven't come across anything particularly traumatic in a Silent Hill sense yet (although I wouldn't be surprised to see that here) I can see the through line to Resident Evil.
The action is smooth, accurate, and rewarding—which surprised me as I usually don't vibe with 2D gunplay, sometimes the controls are too finicky, but it certainly works here. Head-shotting the zombies is incredibly satisfying, as is kicking them to the floor and beating them with a baseball bat.
Then there are the puzzles. I didn't come across too many, but the ones I did find were very rewarding. It's not rocket science, but the solutions aren't always obvious either. They are, however, very intuitive; you can do a lot with a little, something I very much appreciate.
But my favourite aspect of The Road of Dust and Sorrow has to be just how cool this post-apocalyptic world is. Maybe it's the pixel art, but it manages to look dilapidated and creepy while also being oddly pretty to look at. I was searching an abandoned warehouse full of zombies and rotting cargo while thinking to myself that with a bit of elbow grease this place could really scrub up.
If you want pretty and cosy, though, the campervan is where it's at. I didn't spend as much time as I would have liked to there, but it managed to feel like a real home—the only safe place left in this world.

pool.titulo: Former Rockstar environment artist breaks silence: GTA 6 is 'generally stunning,' but Red Dead 2 might have had better rivers
pool.resumen: "I want to celebrate this world that I spent literal years working on."
pool.contenido:
David O'Reilly, an environment artist who worked at Rockstar for 12 years on games like Red Dead Redemption 2, Grand Theft Auto 5, and the just-released GTA 6, recently started a YouTube channel called Game World Art where he explores videogame environments. For the last year and a half or so, he's chatted about those games and others from his point of view, sharing tidbits about the tech involved in making them—and now that GTA 6 is out, he's showing off his work and offering some impressions.
"To set expectations, this is not a Rockstar insider-type channel, it's not telling you exactly how Rockstar makes their worlds, this is more about seeing these kinds of open world games—and this one in particular—through my eyes and my perspective as an environment artist," he said in the video.
In his impressions video, he cruises around for a while and talks about his changing relationship to Rockstar games. Given that putting them together was literally his day job, he couldn't enjoy games like RDR 2 and GTA 5 "to anywhere near the extent" that can enjoy GTA 6—since he left the studio in 2023, he's got some distance from the final game. That doesn't mean he's turning the analytical part of his brain off entirely, though, as he stopped here and there to critique the world he saw.
He called the game's art "generally stunning" and "almost flawless," saying it was visually better than Crimson Desert, which was hamstrung by a "slight jankiness." But he also said he preferred RDR 2's rivers, which he worked on extensively to the point that it became a specialty. If you think he's being persnickety, he did note that he's "obsessed with rivers," and has argued in a previous video that Crimson Desert's rivers "just clinch it" over Red Dead's. Hopefully we can get a definitive river tier list from O'Reilly soon to settle matters on a broader scale.
Still, he had almost exclusively positive things to say, and was careful to note that it's hard for any one artist to take credit for anything on a game as huge in scope as a Rockstar open world heist-'em-up. Ultimately, it seems like he's mostly pleased to see his and his friends' work finally out in the open: "I want to celebrate this world that I spent literal years working on. And I have plenty of friends who are still at Rockstar who have worked on this for a long time, and I couldn't be more pleased for you all."

pool.titulo: How to unlock the Brooks Boatworks safe in GTA 6
pool.resumen: And find a new gun, lots of pills and plenty of cash.
pool.contenido:
GTA 6 drops you into Chapter 2 desperate for cash, but you'll quickly find a few opportunities to make a quick buck if you don't mind trying to outrun bullets. One of the ways that you can get flush quickly is by visiting Brooks Boatworks , a criminal enterprise that's full of pills, cash and explosives. You'll also find a safe in need of a code, which I can help you find.
A word of warning, though: the boatworks is heaving with gun-toting crooks, and getting into a big firefight is just going to bring the cops down on you. Stealth is absolutely a good choice here, but I also recommend going in heavily armed. You can complete the heist just with Lucia, but it's going to be tougher.
Brooks Boatworks location You can find Brooks Boatworks in the north of Port Gellhorn , just to the right of the larger bridge. When you get near the main gate, guards will start threatening you. Even if you take them out, you're not getting in that way.
Instead, head to the right where there's an unlocked gate. You'll still need to get through the fence to get into the boatworks, but that's simple. Right in front of you when you come through the gate you'll find a big gap in the fence. Just walk through it. This also gives you a decent view of the boatworks. If you want to go in loud, this is a great place to take out some goons with a long-ranged weapon.
Brooks Boatworks safe code location Near where you got through the fence, you'll find the smallest building in the compound. This should be your first port of call. Inside you'll find cash, medicine and a unique carbine— the Clunker . It's a solid all-rounder. Once you grab your new toy, check out the map on the wall behind it. Not only will you find the code for the boatworks safe, you'll find other safe codes as well.
Looking at the map will save the codes, so now you know 6823 is the magic number .
Brooks Boatworks safe location You'll find the safe inside the warehouse—it's the largest building, so you can't miss it. There are lots of ways to get inside the warehouse, but I recommend the sneaky route. On the right side of the warehouse, you'll find a way up onto the roof . Once you get up, just climb over it and you'll find an opening that lets you drop in from above.
Now you're at the top of the warehouse, but you'll need to go down to find the room with the safe. Head down, but stick to the side you entered from, and you'll find a room with a pool table and some goons —this is where you'll find the safe.
Just pop in the code 6823 and grab the cash.
Don't leave Brooks Boatworks just yet If you're not close to death or being hounded by cops yet, take some time to explore the rest of the compound. There's cash and pills just scattered all over the place, and make sure to grab all the explosive weaponry, especially the launcher that's just chilling on the top floor , above the room with the safe.
Once you've cleared the warehouse, you'll find yet another building to the west. There's more to find here, including another safe . This one can be broken into without a code, thankfully. Now you can bounce and go on a shopping spree!

pool.titulo: Rockstar Says Jason's Viral Personality in GTA 6 Comes From Steve McQueen and Real-Life Veterans
pool.resumen: Rockstar Games has opened up about GTA 6 protagonist Jason's viral personality and the two specific inspirations that helped bring him to life.
pool.contenido:
Rockstar Games has opened up about GTA 6 protagonist Jason's viral personality and the two specific inspirations that helped bring him to life.
As 13 years of waiting for the next Grand Theft Auto ended last week, players have found themselves enamored with Jason Duval. Stoic, nonchalant, calm, composed, resigned; whatever you want to call one of GTA 6's new protagonists, Rockstar says it carefully crafted his already iconic demeanor by pulling from a Steve McQueen classic and real-life veterans.
The studio's senior vice president of narrative, Rupert Humphries, talked about how the studio behind the mega-hit video game built Jason from the ground up during a conversation with Destructoid . Centering the story on a "couple on the run" marked new territory for Rockstar, but it's far from a new concept in entertainment. So, the team turned to movies, particularly Sam Peckinpah's The Getaway.
"Steve McQueen was famous for pulling lines out of scripts and saying things with his presence alone," Humphries explained. "We wanted to see how close we could get to that with a game character, where so many of our protagonists have been the opposite."
He continued, saying that Rockstar's research into real-world veterans and Army Rangers helped refine its approach. Those who have played the game (and keen-eyed trailer watchers ) already know about Jason's military background, so the influence here definitely tracks.
"These guys typically aren’t running their mouths or reacting to something unless it’s strictly necessary, while still being strong and still asserting themselves."
Jason is the talk of Vice City and has been for some time. As Rockstar shared more details about its seemingly shy lead ahead of GTA 6's launch, some fans began to wonder if he could be the franchise's first-ever neurodivergent protagonist . In addition to his personality, Humphries described Jason as "wired differently" during a recent interview with Love magazine.
While Jason steals more than just wads of cash in Vice City, his partner in crime has proven to be just as impactful. Game writer Michael Wiafe said looking into the kind of criminal activity known to make headlines in Florida was one of the first things the team did when creating both Jason and Lucia. For Rockstar, it wasn't just about creating true-to-life criminals; it was about creating fully realized human beings.
"From then on, it was about coming up with authentic characters that didn’t stray too far from reality but also were not totally bound by it either," Wiafe said. "The majority of our main characters are undeniably reprehensible on paper, full-blown criminals, but also decent human beings. Their moral makeup isn’t necessarily cut-and-dry, and we don’t attempt to make excuses for them. What’s important is how they resonate, no matter where you’re experiencing the game in the world."
Between the chaos of robbing gas stations and drug dealers and getting into high-speed car chases, Jason and Lucia can become quite the power couple. Game writer Elizabeth Gauvey-Kern said to Destructoid, "You really want them to make it." The quiet moments where the duo scrolls through social media in their bed or drives the other one to work can be just as important as the action set pieces. Gauvey-Kern added, "Those need to hit too, and you need to connect with how the characters are feeling in those moments."
Although GTA 6 launched for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S three days ago, Leonida is packed with enough things to do to keep players playing for months. While we wait to see what's next for Rockstar, you can check out IGN's 10/10 review . You can also read about how the developers made every NPC feel like real people you could run into on the street .

pool.titulo: Forget the Lighthouse, GTA 6’s Best Minigame Is a Full-Blown Zombie Shooter That Will Take You Hours To Beat
pool.resumen: Yes, we know you're all playing GTA 6, but don't forget to check out Street Trash 3: Dezombifier, the certified banger on Jason's JoySystem console.
pool.contenido:
To say I was up until midnight last night with GTA 6 is technically correct, but not the full picture. What I was actually doing was headshotting undead nightmares in Street Trash 3: Dezombifier, a moreish isometric twin-stick shooter that lives inside Jason's PS5-alike JoySystem.
You play it briefly with Cal during the story, and it impressed me enough to want to beat it fully. After nearly four hours, I still haven't.
It's clearly inspired by the Sony-published Dead Nation from 2010, but it mashes the zombie slaying with a roguelike deckbuilder. Every time an enemy squelches, their blood splattering the pavement, you gain XP, and at each new level you pick a card to adjust your build. Basic cards boost movement speed, fire rate, damage or critical hit chance, but rarer cards transform your tactics, such as one that doubles your damage given and received.
Your goal is to collect six gears strewn around a deceptively large map and leave via a rooftop chopper. You'll die a lot, but on each run you'll learn a little more about the world's layout and discover new cards to experiment with.
The satisfaction of Street Trash 3 is in crafting a build on the fly from the cards you're dealt, and in feeling your power spiral. You're constantly levelling up and that escalation, the way your build rapidly grows and branches depending on what you find, reminds me a lot of Vampire Survivors . Like that game, it's most fun when you lean into a specific skill: the closest I've come to victory was when I swapped my pistol for a micro-SMG, buffing and buffing my fire rate until the bullets streamed like a deadly snake.
I also got deep on a run boosting my speed and stamina so I could infinitely sprint from groups of enemies, and another where – inspired by a detailed Reddit thread discussing the best builds – I found a card that improved my critical chance by 50% while standing still. When combined with other critical hit cards, I could basically stand in the same spot and mow down everything down around me, painting a gruesome circle of guts.
There is so much craft that most players simply won't see, so many developer hours spent creating missable moments of delight. It is ludicrous that something as meaty and polished as Street Trash 3 exists inside another video game – and even more ludicrous that it's one of three games you can play on Jason's console (Rockstar told Kotaku that "an internal dev team within the dev team" makes these games).
But, like in real life, not every game available for the JoySystem is a banger. Of the three games on Jason’s hard drive, Time Jackers Rewind is the most forgettable. It's a stylish top-down shooter that plays a bit like a slower, sci-fi, less-good Hotline Miami . I appreciate how its checkpoints are tantalizingly spread far enough that you can't just sprint between them, close enough that after every death I was sure I was seconds away. Sadly its best weapon, a concussive shotgun that rumbles your controller, runs out of ammo after just a few seconds, and it's tricky to see enemies among all the on-screen effects.
Tenenbrae Lux is the third, a joke about auteurs stretched into an entire puzzle game. The developer is Johannes Zuch, a clear play on The Witness developer Jonathan Blow (Zuch/Suck, get it?), and his name is listed 38 times during the end credits, including as "architect as perception" and "left stick sensitivity tension consultant". This, surely, is a send-up of Hideo Kajima popping up multiple times in his own credits. The looping stairway in its central puzzle evokes Kojima's P.T. but if you squint you can also see riffs on Alan Wake, Dear Esther, and Robert Eggers’ black-and-white 2019 film The Lighthouse.
As a puzzler, it's intriguing. I say intriguing rather than fun because I can't say I really enjoyed it. The narrator's dialogue is deliberately grandiloquent and recondite ("Hark! An unearthly sound beckons. Like the sirens call, I am fated to find its source"), and the central puzzle is mind-bendingly complicated. Without completley spoiling it, you must loop through a series of rooms in a bunker and spot anomalies, cross-reference them with other clues to assign them a number, and then arrange those numbers in chronological order using a calendar in each room.
Rewarding when you've solved it, for sure, but a pain when you're trying.
The whole thing takes a couple of hours to complete, less if you look up the strategy guides than now exist across the internet (although note that the bunker puzzle is different for each player). And so if you want to beat all of the games on Jason's console, then, you'll need roughly five hours at the very least. That's a pretty impressive amount of game that's not Grand Theft Auto 6 in your copy of Grand Theft Auto 6.
What I love most about these three games is that they are entirely optional, like the majority of GTA 6. There is so much craft that most players simply won't see, so many developer hours spent creating missable moments of delight, so many systems I haven't yet engaged with. It speaks to both Rockstar's budget and its confidence, and as a player it's comforting to know that pretty much wherever I turn I'll find something hand-crafted and surprising. No matter how much time I put in, I couldn't possibly see everything.
What I can do, though, is see everything in Street Trash 3: Dezombifier. Back in I wade, for one more run.

pool.titulo: American Psycho Remake From Director Luca Guadagnino No Longer Happening
pool.resumen: Director Luca Guadagnino has confirmed his American Psycho remake is officially dead.
pool.contenido:
Director Luca Guadagnino has confirmed his American Psycho remake is officially dead.
The Challengers and Call Me by Your Name movie maker delivered the disappointing news when asked for an update on Deadline's Crew Call podcast. He admitted the script for the project that he read, which was penned by the writer behind The Bourne Ultimatum and Side Effects, was "fantastic" but not something he can continue working on.
"American Psycho, which is a fantastic script from Scott Z. Burns, unfortunately, is not happening for me, as we speak," Guadagnino said.
Guadagnino has more than proven himself as a name capable of handling the weight of a property on the level of American Psycho, which is exactly why movie fans were so excited to hear he could be attached to the project in 2024. Although fans have referred to what would have become his slice into the well-established movie universe as a 'remake,' at the time of its announcement, Lionsgate teased that the project would have been more of an adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis' American Psycho novel, rather than a remake of Christian Bale's 2000 movie .
Updates on Guadagnino's American Psycho have been few and far between in the years since its announcement, though. Elvis star Austin Butler was once in the running for the role of Patrick Bateman, as was Euphoria's Jacob Elordi. It was reported in October 2025 that the film would not gender-swap its lead role .
Bale eventually went on to comment on Guadagnino's reimagining and another actor bringing his iconic character to the big screen. He said "all the best to 'em" just earlier this year, adding, "I like brave people."
The director didn't explain why his version of American Psycho won't be moving forward, just that it's "not happening for me." While that means any version of American Psycho won't be coming to movies anytime soon, it's unclear if Lionsgate has completely closed the door on Patrick Bateman. With Burns' script finished, there's always the chance a different filmmaker could take the reins.
For now, though, it's best to assume the American Psycho remake/adaptation is well and truly dead. In the meantime, Guadagnino is gearing up for the release of his Sam Altman biopic, Artificial . The film is gearing up for a limited premiere Christmas 2026 before getting a wider release January 8, 2027.

pool.titulo: GTA 6 needed a dedicated team to make sure all its different body types could share animations: 'It was a huge team effort'
pool.resumen: Making sure your animations don't break while you're cultivating mass.
pool.contenido:
We don't know precisely how big GTA 6's "big boy" budget was, but let's put aside the alarming excess of contemporary mass-consumption entertainment for a moment and talk about the real big boy: bulked up Jason.
While GTA 6's body morphing might not go quite as far (in terms of waistband measurements) as its predecessor San Andreas—or even a game like Fable 2—it does boast extensive variety of different body shapes among its cast, and making that work at such a high level of visual fidelity took an entire dedicated team.
In an interview with IGN , Rockstar vice president of animation Mark Tennant said it was an early decision in development to "push the variation in character sizes and body types … This required us to establish a very robust way to share animations between characters while still resolving multiple points of contact, such as most vehicle interactions and grappling in hand-to-hand combat."
It also took eschewing a "traditional approach" in favor of "new techniques," the sort I imagine you can only implement at Rockstar levels of budget and manpower. "We also had to grow a team dedicated to overseeing the implementation, which required close collaboration with the art and rigging teams," said Tennant. "All these aspects needed to come together to make it work, so it was a huge team effort."
In the same IGN piece, senior technical art director Valmor Garcia said the ultimate goal was to ensure each character had "singular awareness and visual identities," which included giving them unique faces and anatomy (the six-figure animation count is part of that too, I imagine). All the blood, sweat, and so on seem to be paying off given the game's absolutely massive launch , but Saints Row 3 is still the only crime sandbox that lets me replace all my character's dialog with meaningless zombie grunts , so it's impossible to say which is better.

pool.titulo: New Dota 2 patch tries to help games end faster, adds an item that summons super creeps in every lane at once
pool.resumen: It's awfully reminiscent of ideas you can find in other, more fast-paced MOBAs.
pool.contenido:
The longest game of Dota I've played was comfortably past the 70-minute mark. Matches that gloriously long-winded can be fun in small doses, but they can also be exhausting and infuriating—this is Dota we're talking about, after all. The latest patch to rearrange the venerable MOBA, 7.42, is finally here , and it's got tons of changes that might just prevent your games from going feature length.
The most exciting of these, for my money, is the Greater Horn of Battle: a guaranteed drop from the Tormentor neutral monster that summons a wave of super creeps in all your team's lanes (the patch notes refer to them as the more powerful mega creeps, but players have noted the stats don't match up that way). If you've played League of Legends or Deadlock, it fills a niche similar to the Rift Herald or Deadlock's Unstable Rifts—an objective you can complete in the earlier stages of a game to push lane(s) hard.
It's an ability that, if timed correctly, could force the other team to scramble to protect each lane or risk losing lots of ground. And it's not the only change with the potential to speed up matches.
Base hero health has gone up from 120 to 200, with the caveat that strength now gives less health per point, meaning that heroes will be sturdier early on but slightly squishier later. The Glyph of Fortification, a teamwide spell that makes buildings invulnerable, no longer resets its cooldown when certain buildings go down. Heroes also now gain experience passively, even when dead, meaning that you never completely stop growing stronger as the match progresses.
It will probably take some time to see if this actually meaningfully reduces match times or if these changes even stick around for long, but personally, anything that makes Dota a little bit speedier has the potential to reignite my passion for the game. Whenever I dip in these days, it's to play the fastest mode possible—Turbo, which accelerates every aspect of play and gives you oodles of gold just for existing—but it's so different from the traditional Dota setup that it may as well be a new game.

pool.titulo: GTA 6 discourse is suffering from the flat earther effect
pool.resumen: Didn't you hear? You can't even steal cars anymore.
pool.contenido:
If you ever watch science videos on social media, you've probably been served a video of someone debunking the claims of a flat earther.
It starts with a clip of some belligerent dope demanding to know why, if the earth is so round, ships don't disappear over the horizon. A greenscreened science communicator then appears, rubs their forehead, and shows us a video of a ship disappearing over the horizon. Checkmate.
It's good content, but if you linger too long on one of those videos, you'll get another, and then another, and pretty soon your whole feed will be debunking videos. Now you're enrolled in a never ending lesson plan which features such insights as 'an all-meat diet is not good for you,' 'the moon landing was real,' and 'hating women is not in fact based .'
The total effect of this is that the most ignorant and dishonest quacks and provocateurs get to set the level of discourse, and instead of investigating new metaphorical horizons in topics that interest you, you wind up watching people debate the existence of the actual horizon.
Which brings me to Grand Theft Auto 6. Despite making $3.79 billion on its launch day, it's easy to stumble across confident social media claims that it's a total flop and everyone's going to refund it. According to popular X posts, GTA 6 doesn't even let you steal cars anymore, and there are hundreds of Metacritic user reviewers insisting that it's far-left propaganda rather than the mass-market entertainment product it obviously is.
It's the videogame discourse version of flat eartherism. The millions of people playing GTA 6 do not think it is a "cuck simulator" because you can buy a woman flowers, but it's hard not to react to the few dorks making that claim, even though focusing on debunking them severely limits the depth of the conversations we can then have about the game. Good luck discussing your feelings if you dislike GTA 6 for normal reasons!
Over the past few days, I've entertained sparks of hope that GTA 6 could be the flashpoint that brings us out of this era of videogame discourse. The millions of people playing it and not reacting like buffoons are surely irrefutable evidence that culture war dunces don't represent the masses.
But then again, we're still pointing at videos of ships going over the horizon to prove that the earth isn't flat.

The casino in GTA 6 is closed. Trust me, I tried every door, and the only one that opened was a utility closet.
I was early into my playthrough, still in Chapter 1 of the GTA 6 story missions , so I thought maybe there'll be some mission that unlocks the casino so I can play some poker, try my luck at the slots, and maybe bet on the also-closed dog track—I assume it's a dog track because I've seen dogs in GTA 6, but no horses—that's right next door to the casino.
Nope! I'm now 100% done with the main story and that casino is still closed. And that's not the only business in GTA 6 that isn't open for business. Not even a half-mile away from the casino there's a go-cart track called Hot Skidz sporting a huge "Coming Soon" sign. I saw that early in my game as well, and checked back later. Still closed. I also found a second, smaller casino. Also closed.
What a letdown. I managed to get my motorcycle onto the go-cart track, and as I drove glumly around it, alone, having no fun, I perked up a bit. Maybe this just gives me something to look forward to. A hint of more singleplayer content that'll be coming to GTA 6 next year. Hopefully next year.
There's already a lot of seemingly unfinished stuff in GTA 6, partial systems that could be added to and completed, like:
I can throw a frisbee but no one will catch it—not even dogs—or throw it back I can go to a tennis court, pick up a tennis racket and tennis ball, and hit the ball with the racket, but I can't actually play tennis Speaking of dogs, who would put so many dogs in a game and not let me have my own dog? There's a baseball bat and baseballs, but I can't play baseball The dog thing is madness. Gotta let us have dogs at some point There are so many cool houses but I can only live in the one currently assigned to me by the story There are hotels everywhere but I can't rent a room You can play eight-ball pool but not nine-ball? Pure insanity, even moreso than the dog decision There's tons of construction sites, so many it can't just be satire about America's horrible infrastructure, they've gotta at least build a new few things for us to play with Like, no offense to the snake, but I want a damn dog I felt better after that, but as I went back to stare at that huge, closed casino—which is all lit up at night like it's actually open, even though it is not open, and I know this because I rechecked all the doors—I remembered how the casino in GTA 5 worked. It came to the game post launch, but only as part of GTA Online. It never opened in singleplayer.
But surely, why include the building at all in GTA 6 singleplayer if it wasn't also going to be in singleplayer? They wouldn't do that to us, would they? They wouldn't open it in GTA 6 Online and not open it in GTA 6 singleplayer.
That would be like putting dozens of dogs in a game and not letting us have our own dog. Madness.

pool.titulo: Scott Lynch, author of The Lies of Locke Lamora, has 1,493 hours in Star Wars: Rebellion and 1,564 in BattleTech: 'If J.R.R. Tolkien had had a Steam account, his numbers would be pretty embarrassing too'
pool.resumen: The fantasy novelist guides us through the games on his PC.
pool.contenido:
Disk Cleanup Welcome to Disk Cleanup , our regular weekend feature delving into the PCs of PC gaming luminaries. Come back every weekend to read a new interview, digging into the important questions, like "How tidy is your desktop?" and "What game will you never uninstall?"
Playing on school computers has been a rite of passage for many young PC gamers, whether through dedicated edutainment titles or rogue installations by chancing pupils. But fantasy novelist Scott Lynch went one step further: he took the school computers home.
"My mother worked for our school district, so I'd occasionally have the chance to sneak into the computer lab, or we would borrow and Apple II over the summer," Lynch says. "When we did that, I borrowed Infocom games … text-only adventure games from the '80s like Zork, Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, Planetfall, A Mind Forever voyaging. I was really into those when I was about 12."
Text-based adventures would eventually become a defining feature of Lynch's life, albeit in a different format. His debut novel, The Lies of Locke Lamora , was published in 2006, charting the schemes and adventures of a group of master con artists called The Gentleman Bastards. Two further novels in The Gentleman Bastard Sequence have since followed: 2007's Red Seas Under Red Skies , and 2013's The Republic of Thieves
Lynch currently working on a novella in the same world called More Than Fools Fill Graves, as well as his highly anticipated fourth novel, The Thorn of Emberlain. "It is something that I am absolutely working on and trying to be as open and honest about as possible," he says. But he took a quick break from writing elaborate fantasy heists to show me around the treasure-filled vault of his Steam library.
What game are you currently playing? I have reopened Morrowind for the first time in a number of years. Right around the time I was working on my first novel and had not finished it yet, I was playing it on the original Xbox. Other than the fact I was like 23, 24, I can't fathom how I did that.
I've been meaning to go back to Morrowind for ages, but I was put off by the jankiness of the UI, the quality-of-life experience, or the thought that there were just enough rough edges of this game that's now nearly a quarter of a century old, that I wouldn't enjoy it.
I was talking to another author who maybe has a bad computer game habit, and he turned me on to OpenMW. He posted some screenshots on Bluesky of some beautiful-looking Morrowind vistas and some nice skies and vegetation. And I thought "A-ha! Here's a man that uses mods." So even though I own a copy of Morrowind, like the fourth copy I've bought in my life, I'm now using OpenMW, and I'm loving it.
The thing that I enjoy about Morrowind is the incredible granularity of its various subsystems and the game-breaking things that you can do with processes like alchemy and enchantment. And the fact you can enchant layers of clothing and be wearing enchanted underwear underneath your enchanted armour. [But] I set a bunch of rules for my character, because usually I play something along the lines of a wizard who can go anywhere, do anything, build high-powered potions to fly all over the landscape at high speed.
I decided that I would play something along the template of a Paladin, and I gave myself a very limited powerset that I could create utilising the custom spell-builders … so I have a very limited toolset, and I opted to spend more time actually wandering around the world doing quests, and less time sitting in one place making 10,000 potions.
I played Skyrim to death [with] many character concepts, and one of my favourites was a little ruleset that I called the Conan playthrough, where you play as melee-type character who cannot use magic at all … you place all these rules and limitations upon yourself. What I found is that narrowing the focus of the game experience can be as liberating as having a completely open world before you, and I've rediscovered that with this particular Morrowind playthrough.
What was the previous game you played, and is it still installed? It's a game from the late '90s called Star Wars: Rebellion, which over in the UK would have been known as Star Wars: Supremacy. It's elderly, it's janky, its UI and its quality of life are from a previous era of human development. It's absolutely full of problems. But it's also got kernels of brilliance, and there's never been anything like it ever since. As a Star Wars fan, I find myself returning to it over and over, as a dog to his vomit.
What is the oldest game (by release date) currently installed on your PC? I've still got Master of Orion 2 , and it's still playable, which is from '90s. I love MOO2. I've played it to death in every possible permutation. I last played Master of Orion about five years ago. That would have also been in the pandemic.
You can see how nearly every game in the 4X space has been trying for the last three decades to, in some fashion, be that game and recreate its experience, and that's a very difficult thing to do … MOO2 just has a certain smoothness to it.
I've tried to get into other 4X games … but I just don't think that any 4X space game since MOO2 has successfully emulated that smoothness of pickup and that open sense of play, as in "Where's my civilization going to go?"
To a certain extent when you play a game like MOO2, outside the bounds of creating a custom species and a custom culture, you're playing with somebody else's IP, and when I play a game like that, I look for a certain degree of possessiveness, a certain degree of personalisation. I want to play my species' story and I don't necessarily want to play with somebody else's narrative IP.
What is the highest number of hours you have in any given game, according to Steam? All right, let's look at the embarrassing total. All I'm going to say about this is that if J.R.R Tolkien had had a Steam account, his numbers would be pretty embarrassing too.

pool.titulo: Rockstar Says Darts Were Cut From GTA 6 Because It Didn't Have 'Unlimited Money or Time' to Make It 'Feel Proper'

pool.contenido:
Rockstar Games crammed a lot of content into GTA 6 , but fan-favorite mini-games like darts and bowling didn't make the cut because the team didn't have "unlimited money or unlimited time" to do those activities justice.
Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson explained why the studio chose to focus on some aspects of development and not others during an interview with VGC . As noted by the site, picking up a game of darts has proven to be a good pastime in games like GTA 5 and GTA Online, but in GTA 6, the standards were a bit higher.
From NPCs to the feel of motorized scooters, Leonida is Rockstar's most realistic playground yet. Every blade of grass was given special attention, and while pool was one game the team was able to fully realize, not everything panned out like they had hoped. Nelson said "darts was a contentious one" when talking about the decision to cut it from the game, explaining that it was left behind because the team didn't have the resources to do it right.
"Even we… you hear they have unlimited money or unlimited time, even we do not and so sometimes you just have to admit we are not going to be able to make this to the level we feel we need to," he said.
Nelson elaborated, saying that, starting with Red Dead Redemption 2, the team started to treat mini-games more like activities. In other words, bonuses like darts became less about being a diversion of Rockstar's open worlds and more of an extension of them. The goal is to make pool, darts, or any other activity feel like it's just as punchy and weighty for Jason and Lucia as it is in the real world.
Using GTA 6's in-game workouts as an example, he added, "You’re not just pushing a button; it mimics what weightlifting is."
"A lot of work [is needed] to get it tuned right," Nelson continued. "Darts is one we just didn’t get to."
Long story short, Rockstar just "didn't have the resources" to make it "feel proper." His thoughts on the matter – or any scenario where a mechanic or activity is cut – were summed up in one line: "It’s better not to do it than to do it and have it not be good enough."

As of the latest update, the AI-generated music is gone. "It's a little sad given Joey Kuras (game's sound designer) did some excellent sounds for Mewgenics", ShweetStuff wrote, "but I suppose this is the industry nowadays!"

pool.titulo: SNEG has re-released three more venerable PC strategy games including Warlords 4: Heroes of Etheria
pool.resumen: Let the war begin.
pool.contenido:
As well as giving a spit-and-polish digital release to various Warhammer classics , antique D&D games , and the cult ellipsoid horror games in the Ecstatica series , SNEG has been bug-fixing a bunch of strategy games from years gone by and getting them up on Steam and GOG. The latest trio to appear on digital platforms are Theocracy, Soldiers at War, and Warlords 4: Heroes of Etheria.
Warlords 4 was the final turn-based game in the beloved series, with the RTS spin-off series Warlords Battlecry already two games deep by the time of its release in 2003. This updated version supports resolutions up to 4K, and incorporates community fixes and a community-made campaign. It's available on Steam and GOG .
Soldiers at War took the X-COM/UFO turn-based tactics formula—this was 1998, X-COM still had a hyphen—and applied it to World War II. You'd choose a squad of eight from your platoon of 32 each mission, fighting through a campaign that started in North Africa and ended in Germany, gaining experience along the way. SNEG's version supports 1280x720 widescreen resolution. It's available on Steam and GOG .
Theocracy narrowly beat Total War to the punch in March of 2000 with its mix of turn-based civilization management and real-time battles, tasking you with uniting Aztec tribes before the prophesied Spanish invasion. You're on the clock with 100 years to use diplomacy, trade, and warfare to bring together an empire that can stand the test of time. The updated version still has a resolution of 800x600, but uses FSR 1 to scale up for modern displays. You'll be shocked to learn, it's also available on Steam and GOG .
All three games are designed to be easy to run on modern Windows systems, and have cloud saves and achievements. I'm tempted by Warlords 4, which I didn't play at the time because I'd moved over to the real-time Battlecry games by then. But I've still got fond memories of Warlords 2 Deluxe, which had 60 different worlds so if you were tired of raising griffon armies in its generic fantasy land you could conquer something oddball like Dante's Inferno instead. Or even make your own, right down to pixel-crafting the unit art. Good times.

pool.titulo: Nvidia released a hotfix for its driver hammering your SSD, but it doesn't actually work
pool.resumen: AI isn't great at fixing problems AI created.
pool.contenido:
Over the last couple of weeks, some Nvidia users noticed their SSDs were taking a hammering , reporting their driver's log file was being overwritten constantly, sometimes to the tune of 30 GB every hour. Which obviously isn't great for the lifespan of the valuable SSD you've got it installed on.
Given the problem was caused by recent driver updates, rolling back to version 621.01 was the best solution until Nvidia could do something about it. Which they did, releasing a hotfix as version 621.35 . It's not available in the GeForce app yet, but you can download it directly from Nvidia's site. Not that you should.
As users on the Nvidia subreddit are reporting, the problem persists. While the hotfix reduces the peak write rate and prevents it for a short while after reboot, it eventually creeps back in. One user reported that overnight the log file was still being rewritten by approximately 4.5 GB every hour.
So yeah, the best solution remains to roll back to version 621.01 and, as always with Nvidia drivers, to hold off on updating to the latest driver until it's been confirmed safe. If this ongoing saga sounds familiar, it's because the same thing happened to AMD's GPU drivers earlier this month. Maybe vibecoding driver updates and then vibecoding fixes for their inevitable bugs isn't the best way of doing things.

pool.titulo: GTA 6 The End of the Road: Should you swim for it, or choose no surrender?
pool.resumen: A choice (or two!) can lead to drastically different endings.

Please note, this guide contains massive spoilers for some of the endings of Grand Theft Auto 6 . If you don't want to know what happens, please stop reading!
There are multiple endings to GTA 6, and not all the endings take place in the same location. One of the potential final scenes during the GTA 6 story mission , The End of the Road, takes place on a bridge in the Leonida Keys.
After discovering the cops are onto them, Jason and Lucia drive away from Cal's house and head to Brian's marina to find an airplane. The police quickly trap them on a bridge with a roadblock ahead and multiple cars behind them. Lucia wants to keep going but Jason thinks it's all over for them. The player is then given a choice, "Swim for it" or "No Surrender."
AGAIN, MASSIVE SPOILERS BELOW! STOP NOW IF YOU DON'T WANT TO KNOW THE ENDINGS !
No Surrender Jason and Lucia decide Tomas is better off without them in his life. They drive through the roadblock, shooting at the cops. They're both shot to death and we see them dead in the front seat of the car, still holding hands. During the end credits, we see Tomas living happily with Lucia's sister and her husband and children.
Swim for it (A, B, and C) Jason and Lucia decide to jump off the bridge and swim to freedom.
However, a second choice appears once you've chosen 'Swim for it.' As Jason gets out of the car, a prompt for Lucia to 'Exit' the car appears. You can choose for Lucia to follow through with the plan by pressing the button, or change your mind and let the prompt expire.
A: 'Swim for it' and 'Exit' : The couple will get out of the car together and walk to the edge of the bridge. Lucia jumps but Jason does not, letting himself get arrested by the cops. During the credits, Lucia signs the deal which keeps her free and sends Jason to prison. We see her bring Tomas to visit him, so Jason finally meets his son, though it's through glass.
B: 'Swim for it' and don't 'Exit' : If you choose to swim for it but don't choose the 'Exit' prompt, Jason will get out of the car but Lucia will remain in the car. The police will open fire and kill them both. As with the No Surrender option, we see Tomas living with Lucia's sister's family.
C: 'Swim for it' and 'Exit' (with $2 million in Buck Me savings) : If you delayed the Protective Custody mission of GTA 6 until you had deposited $2 million in savings, the Swim for it and Exit choices will show the same results, but during the credits, Lucia uses the money to get Jason released from prison. Lucia picks him up at prison, and Jason meets Tomas and holds his hand.
Note: These are not the only endings to GTA 6. I've seen several more endings that do not take place on the bridge at all and don't involve these particular choices.

pool.titulo: Unreal Engine 6 to jettison key scripting feature earlier than planned in favor of AI coding
pool.resumen: Bye-bye, Blueprints.
pool.contenido:
Unreal Engine 6 will not launch with the engine's long-standard Blueprints scripting system. The news came in a Friday, November 19 post on the Unreal Engine website , written by Epic Games executive vice president of development, Marcus Wassmer. Here's Wassmer's top-level summary from the post:
Blueprints have not (and it appears, will not) be deprecated in Unreal Engine 5, and the company maintains that projects will still be easy to convert from UE5 to UE6. Wassmer cited a declining cost in AI task completion as one reason for this belief, as well as the team's ongoing, but apparently successful conversion of Fortnite's Blueprint library to UE6's Verse programming language through an AI-assisted process.
Blueprints are a widely-used feature of Unreal. Former Valve developer Chet Faliszek, an AI skeptic, has put out a vlog on the subject . Essentially, Faliszek argues that Blueprints (and features like them in other game engines) represent a middle ground between artistic and technical work, an introduction and skill builder for less technically-minded developers. Without them, such developers seemingly have to either learn Verse code, or integrate LLM prompting into their workflows.
"We made a new skill in the middle there, between normal and expert," Faliszek said of intermediate tools like Blueprints. "To lose that determinism from game design, and instead have to prompt AI⁠—or write your own Verse … It's losing those tools that made all those designers and all those artists so powerful, to be able to do really powerful things and have access to really deep-down things, but in a safe way that the engineers can decide what that meant to them."
A dark horse game of the year candidate, the first-person RPG Queen's Domain , was made with Unreal Engine. I recently spoke to co-developer Eric Berger, who specialized in art and design alongside the more technically-focused Bradley Boothe, a relationship that rhymes with the ones Faliszek outlined in his video.
I spoke to Berger before seeing Epic's latest press release, but Berger already indicated that Unreal's AI pivot is prompting Freshly Baked Games to switch engines for its next project. I followed up with Berger about this Blueprint news, and the developer said that Blueprints were a major part of the workflow on Queen's Domain.
I'm a layman in game development, but I think Wassmer's post elides that there is a large qualitative difference between doing any work via LLM prompt versus the old-fashioned way⁠—I don't like or want to use these tools, myself, and I don't think that's an unpopular stance. Commenter ZILtoid1991 on Faliszek's video compared the move to Apple removing headphone jacks on the iPhone, a comparison I find fruitful.
It was hugely unpopular at the time, and is still derided by enthusiasts, but it also worked . Other manufacturers copied Apple, and everybody has bluetooth headphones now⁠—or Apple's own, proprietary Air Pods. But Apple had far less success trying something similar with its laptops: The lack of ports on late 2010s Macbooks proved disastrous, and Apple has since reintroduced more (and a wider variety of) ports on newer models of the popular line. I certainly have my own anti-AI, pro-headphone jack preferences, but we'll have to see how this plays out with the Unreal Engine.

Tras descubrirse en 1976 por un equipo de arqueólogos, lo más impresionante no es que aún a día de hoy se sigan encontrando restos fantásticamente conservados. Lo realmente increíble es que apenas hemos visto el 15% de todo el edificio.
La culpa la tiene haber parado la investigación del yacimiento, que quedó prácticamente abandonado poco después de ese descubrimiento y que, gracias a un grupo de estudiantes de arqueología , en 2019 volvió a ponerse manos a la obra. Por los frescos encontrados se cree que aquel rincón era una casa señorial en la que los pavos reales, estrechamente ligados a las clases más altas de la estructura social romana, cobran una vital importancia. pool.titulo: Robbing Banks is a Blast, But I Wish There Were More Houses to Repair in GTA 6
pool.resumen: Forget sticking things up with a shotgun, I want to fix things up with a nailgun.
pool.contenido:
My first weekend with Grand Theft Auto 6 was truly mindblowing. The first 20 or so hours I’ve spent with Rockstar’s triumphant return to Vice City have transported me to an impossibly high fidelity game world and treated me to criminal capers so immaculately crafted they make Michael Mann seem more like a Michael mouse. As I’ve made my way across the sprawling Leonida map I’ve relished each and every unethical exploit of lawbreaking lovebirds, Jason and Lucia. So far I’ve been Jason the wheelman, Jason the bagman, and Jason the hitman, but to my surprise, what I really want to be is… Tim the Toolman?
Before you hit me with one of Tim Allen’s trademark quizzical caveman grunts, let me back up for a moment. In case you’re not one of the more than 20 million players who gleefully jumped into Rockstar’s latest crime epic on day one, GTA 6’s opening hours present a number of optional tasks that you can undertake as Jason in an effort to make his girlfriend Lucia’s arrival at your love nest a little more loved-up. You can visit the grocery store to line the kitchen pantry with protein bars and packets of chips, pick up a bouquet of flowers, and even splash out on a customised necklace from a local jeweler if you really want to boost your relationship status to Boyfriend of the Year levels.
I ticked off these tasks more out of open-world obligation than any particularly earnest desire to impress my virtual girlfriend; they were pink dots on my minimap, so my well-trained gamer instincts compelled me to clear them. But what I did derive a surprising amount of satisfaction from, was running down the shortlist of repairs to Jason’s dilapidated waterfront home. Drilling in drywall panels in the bedroom and applying a warm shade of peach-coloured paint to them with a roller. Climbing a ladder onto the roof and fastening fresh shingles to it with a nailgun to stop the ceiling leaks. Replacing the rotten steps leading to the front door with some fresh planks of wood. Each of these tasks provided me with moments of zen far more relaxing than the game's own dedicated meditation minigame. I even took a moment to stop and marvel at the impeccably well-rendered tools in Jason’s shed.
I enjoyed fussing around on Jason’s fixer-upper so much that I must admit I was a little deflated to discover that once this brief burst of renovations are complete, that seems to be it as far as the cosy home makeover minigames are concerned. A lot of the other features of GTA 6 are presented as an appetite-whetting taster before they become ongoing activities to pursue at your leisure for the rest of the story; you go on a short hunting trip with one of Jason’s old army buddies, and from then on you’re free to stalk deer and bears in the Leonida wilderness. You complete a dirt-encrusted drive in an opening event at the Thrillbilly Mud Club, and afterwards you’re free to indulge in spectacular stunt jumps, hill climbs, and a variety of races on the MotorStorm-style circuits.
Completing Jason’s home repairs, however, doesn’t seem to unlock any form of handyman activities to pursue around the map. I envisaged clearing out the longarms and bulletproof vests stashed in the bed of Jason’s truck and loading it up with power tools and paint cans to go do some odd jobs around the neighbourhood – or perhaps even buying run-down properties, fixing them up, and then flipping them to quickly boost Jason and Lucia’s shared bank account. But after speaking with other members of IGN who’ve rolled credits in GTA 6, it doesn’t sound like Jason ever gets another opportunity to pick up his tools again, other than to grab a hammer or shovel to smack hillbillies around with when he’s in the process of stealing the profits from their meth lab.
Now, I know what you’re thinking reading this; if he wanted to do home restorations in a video game, there’s no shortage of quality options out there that could scratch that itch, from The Sims 4 to House Flipper to Powerwash Simulator. I also know what you’re thinking if you happen to be my wife reading this; there’s no shortage of DIY projects I could be spending my Saturday doing around my actual house instead of sitting on the couch complaining of the lack of virtual repair jobs to complete in a video game. (I’ll get to them next weekend, I promise.)
However, I think a big part of the reason that I’d like to do more repairwork in GTA 6 is because this is undoubtedly the most beautiful and believable game world I’ve ever inhabited, and thus I feel an innate urge to preserve it. In fact, unlike any GTA game before it, I’ve found myself really focussing on how much life there is in the environment as opposed to creating my typical trails of death, strapping on a scuba tank and playing with porpoises in the depths of the Atlantic Ocean, or peering at pelicans through the in-game binoculars. I’m only a couple of chapters into the story, but so far I wholeheartedly agree with Luke Reilly’s 10 out of 10 review . GTA 6 is clearly a masterpiece, and one that doesn’t really leave much room for improvement. But, even so, I can’t help but wish it had a few more rooms for improvement.
GTA 6 doesn't leave much room for improvement, but I wish it had a few more rooms for improvement. These are the things I’m thinking about as I drive around Vice City and its surroundings. While most players are probably scanning strip malls for potential stores to rob, I’m eyeballing side streets for run-down homes in need of a fresh coat of paint or a replacement screen door.
